messages.content: What crystalline phase and single-crystal X-ray diffraction temperature are identified for the framework [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol?
The framework is monoclinic with space group C2/c; its single-crystal X-ray diffraction data were obtained at 100 K.

What local Cu coordination environment is found in the framework [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, and what does single-crystal X-ray diffraction alone imply about the Cu oxidation state?

The Cu centers have a distorted tetrahedral geometry coordinated by three BTDAT ligands and one methanol molecule; the O...Cu...N angles are 91.79(15), 95.94(16), and 105.87(16) degrees. Bond-valence sums calculated for assumed Cu(I) and Cu(II) are 1.12 and 1.85, respectively, so crystallography alone cannot discriminate Cu(I) from Cu(II), leaving an intermediate or mixed-valence Cu state possible.
What 2D sheet topology and channel occupancy are present in the framework [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol?

Each BTDAT ligand acts as a three-connecting linker with one cyano arm left uncoordinated. Repetition of these units forms heavily puckered 2D sheets extending in the ab plane. Viewed along the c axis, diamond-shaped channels are apparent and are obstructed by coordinated methanol molecules.

How are the sheets of [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)] packed, where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, and what are the two BTDAT inter-ligand stacking motifs and separations in the crystal?

Interdigitation of BTDAT motifs from individual sheets gives a densely packed framework. BTDAT moieties form pseudo-1D columns parallel to the b axis through two distinct inter-ligand pi-interactions: offset ring-double bond stacking with a mean plane separation of 3.019 Å (S...S 4.000 Å) and slipped face-to-face stacking with a mean plane separation of 3.349 Å (S...S 3.699 Å).

What Cu oxidation-state information is obtained by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for as-synthesized [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, and what does the absence of Cu 2p shake-up satellites imply?

The Cu 2p3/2 spectrum is deconvoluted into components centered at 932.9 and 933.8 eV, assigned to Cu(I) and Cu(II), respectively, with a Cu(I)/Cu(II) ratio of 1.4:1 and an average Cu charge of +1.42. The absence of shake-up satellites is consistent with intrinsic Cu-based mixed valency rather than adventitious surface oxidation.
What framework-level EPR signals identify Cu(II) and radical BTDAT in solid [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol?

The powder EPR spectrum shows characteristic Cu(II) signals at g_parallel and g_perpendicular and a weaker signal at g = 2.00168 attributed to BTDAT radical anion ligands, indicating that Cu(II) and radical BTDAT species are present in the framework.

What optical bands are observed in the diffuse reflectance spectrum of solid [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, and what do they indicate about mixed-valence delocalization?

The solid diffuse reflectance spectrum contains visible bands at 15410, 17140, and 23450 cm-1 assigned to BTDAT radical anion, a band at 20640 cm-1 tentatively assigned to metal-to-ligand charge transfer, and an intense near-infrared band at 6940 cm-1 assignable to intervalence charge transfer, possibly arising from mixed-valence pseudo-1D BTDAT stacks. Applying the semiempirical Hush equation to the intervalence band gives Gamma = 0.77, suggestive of highly valence-delocalized mixed valency.

How do solid-state visible/near-infrared spectroelectrochemical spectra and color of [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, change under cathodic potentials?

In 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate/acetonitrile, the 0 V spectrum shows seven broad bands at 7020, 8560, 9720, 14400, 17190, 20560, and 23240 cm-1; the 14400, 17190, and 20560 cm-1 bands are characteristic of BTDAT radical anion, while the 7020 cm-1 band is assigned to intervalence charge transfer from mixed-valence BTDAT radical anion/dianion species. At -0.25 V all bands decrease in intensity. At -0.45 V the 17190 and 23240 cm-1 bands increase while the near-infrared bands remain unchanged. At -0.70 V the near-infrared bands decrease, and the 14400 and 17190 cm-1 bands also decrease. The solid changes from dark brown/black at 0 V to dark green at -0.45 V and dark red at -0.70 V.

What multi-redox processes are observed for solid [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, by cyclic voltammetry, and how are they assigned?

Cyclic voltammetry of the solid in 0.1 M tetrabutylammonium hexafluorophosphate/acetonitrile at 800 mV/s shows six quasi-reversible processes at -0.479, -0.936, -1.37, -1.73, -2.02, and -2.30 V vs Fc/Fc+. The first four are assigned to sequential one-electron reductions of the BTDAT ligand, while the two most cathodic processes are tentatively assigned to further reductions of BTDAT ligands to 5- and 6- states, possibly stabilized by proximal ligand interactions in the framework.

What pressed-pellet conductivity values and transport interpretation are obtained for [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, between 300 and 195 K?

Four-point probe measurements on a pressed pellet give sigma = 1.9 x 10^-3 S cm-1 at 300 K and sigma = 7.5 x 10^-5 S cm-1 at 195 K, consistent with a non-metallic state. In the linear Arrhenius region, the activation energy is 168 meV. Fits using Efros-Shklovskii or three-dimensional Mott variable-range hopping models do not notably improve on the Arrhenius description, so between 300 and 195 K the conductivity is best described as thermally activated, although lower-temperature mechanisms cannot be ruled out.

What does room-temperature single-crystal electrical transport show for [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, regarding the conductivity magnitude and anisotropy?

Room-temperature single-crystal current-voltage measurements are reasonably linear and give a typical crystal conductivity of about 40 x 10^-6 S cm-1 after correction for crystal dimensions. For rotated placements of the same crystal, the conductivity shows no significant anisotropy, indicating that the dominant conduction pathway is through-bond via the Cu-BTDAT framework.

What temperature-dependent conductivity behavior and activation energy are obtained from variable-temperature single-crystal [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, measurements between 50 and 300 K?

As the temperature is lowered from 300 to 50 K, the single-crystal conductivity decreases and the current-voltage curves show a continuously flattening response, consistent with insulating or semiconducting behavior. A high-temperature Arrhenius fit gives an activation energy of 66 meV. At low temperature the Arrhenius plot becomes nonlinear.

What single-determinant density functional theory predicts for the band structure, orbital character, and dimerized charge-transport pathways of [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol?

Local spin density approximation DFT predicts a metallic electronic structure, with several bands crossing the Fermi energy and a non-zero density of states at E_F. Twelve Frontier bands lie between about -0.5 and +0.7 eV relative to E_F. Integration of the partial density of states over these Frontier bands gives about 0.40 states per Cu, 1.04 states per BTDAT ligand, and 1.56 states per MeOH molecule, per formula unit and per spin, indicating orbitals centered on BTDAT and MeOH plus a third orbital with mixed Cu-MeOH character. Two Frontier bands near 0.5-0.6 eV are mainly BTDAT-derived and disperse quasi-one-dimensionally along the b axis, implying strong BTDAT dimerization with effective intradimer hopping integral t2 about 0.02-0.03 eV and interdimer hopping integral t1 about 0.2-0.3 eV. The remaining ten Frontier bands disperse more uniformly, suggesting a three-dimensional metallic electronic structure with weak anisotropy.

Why is [Cu(BTDAT)(MeOH)], where BTDAT is bis-[1,2,5]-thiadiazolo-tetracyanoquinodimethane and MeOH is methanol, proposed to be a Mott insulator despite DFT metallic bands, and what conductivity mechanism does this imply?

Although single-determinant DFT predicts bands crossing the Fermi energy and therefore metallic behavior, pressed-pellet and single-crystal conductivity measurements show conductivity decreasing as temperature is lowered, indicating activated non-metallic behavior. Because DFT is inconsistent with a band insulator, there is no evidence for a magnetic phase transition, and the sample has little disorder, the most reasonable hypothesis is a Mott-insulating state, an insulator caused by strong electronic correlations; the intervalence charge-transfer band is also consistent with such correlations. This implies incoherent transport rather than band transport, but it does not distinguish between activated transport by Coulombically bound electron-hole pairs and hopping. Strong BTDAT dimerization narrows the Frontier-band width, which may increase the insulating gap and reduce conductivity.

What preparation condition defines the hydrated chromium metal–organic framework with the molybdenum disulfide (mos) network prepared at approximately 33% relative humidity, and what does that relative-humidity value describe?

It is defined by exposing activated single crystals of the chromium mos-topology framework—acetone-exchanged and vacuum-treated at 120 °C for 12 h—overnight at room temperature to a saturated MgCl solution; the ≈33% refers to the relative humidity established by that solution.

In the approximately 33% relative-humidity hydrated state of the chromium metal–organic framework with the molybdenum disulfide (mos) network, what does single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveal about water locations and the state of the voids within the framework layers?

Water inside the pores is significantly disordered and located mainly adjacent to coordinated molecules at the chromium trinuclear nodes through hydrogen bonding, while the voids within the framework layers remain empty.
What crystal system and space group does the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF adopt, and what structural feature accounts for this symmetry?
It crystallizes in the triclinic space group P1. Its asymmetric unit contains two carnosine conformations that are not symmetry-equivalent.
What crystal morphology and size are obtained for the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
It forms hexagonal-prism crystals up to 60 μm long.
Along which crystallographic axis do the solvent-filled channels run in the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The solvent-filled channels run along the a-axis.
What hydrogen-bonding arrangement stabilizes the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF, and does acetonitrile hydrogen-bond to carnosine?

Carnosine groups stack along the channel walls to form an antiparallel β-sheet-like host–host network with N–H···O distances of 2.89 and 2.97 Å. Acetonitrile does not hydrogen-bond to carnosine; carnosine–Zn(II) coordination and the host–host hydrogen bonds stabilize the framework.
What elastic properties were measured for single crystals of the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF by AFM-based nanoindentation?
The Young’s modulus along the crystal thickness direction was 10.97 ± 2.28 GPa, and the corresponding point stiffness was 103.83 ± 26.43 N m⁻¹.
What consequence does triclinic P1 symmetry have for the piezoelectric tensor of the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The P1 structure leaves polarization unconstrained by symmetry, permitting 18 nonzero piezoelectric coefficients.
What piezoelectric strain constants does DFT predict for the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
DFT predicts a longitudinal d33 coefficient of 4.7 pC/N and six other piezoelectric strain coefficients between 9.8 and 18.2 pC/N.
What were the largest effective piezoelectric coefficients measured by PFM for the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF, and how did they compare with DFT predictions?
The largest effective longitudinal coefficient was 4.7 pm/V, and the largest effective shear coefficient was 15.5 pm/V. The corresponding DFT-predicted maxima were 4.7 and 18.2 pm/V.
Along which crystallographic direction is the maximum predicted piezoelectric polarization found in the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF, and how is it related to the guest molecules?
The maximum predicted polarization is −0.33 C/m² along the a-axis, coinciding with the directional alignment of the 3.9 D acetonitrile molecular dipoles in the channels.
How does interionic spacing relate to the predicted axial polarization of the acetonitrile-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?

The predicted axial polarization is inversely proportional to the interionic spacing, which is 6 Å along a, 10 Å along b, and 8 Å along c. The a-axis consequently has the largest predicted axial polarization and the most significant piezoelectric charge coefficients.
What space group and asymmetric-unit composition characterize the isopropanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
It crystallizes in the monoclinic space group P2₁ and contains one isopropanol guest molecule and one neutral zinc–carnosinate complex per asymmetric unit.
What crystal habit is observed for the isopropanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
It forms triangular-prism crystals.
What Zn–carnosine connectivity builds the porous framework of the isopropanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
Each carnosine linker connects four Zn cations, two of which are bridged by a deprotonated imidazole group, producing a permanent microporous scaffold.
What carnosine protonation state and Zn(II) coordination geometry characterize the isopropanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The carboxyl and imidazole groups of carnosine are deprotonated. Each Zn(II) center is tetrahedrally coordinated by a carboxylate group, an amino-terminal group, and two imidazole nitrogen atoms.
What longer-range channel motif occurs in the isopropanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
Reverse-interdigitated T-shaped carnosine linkers form lozenge-shaped one-dimensional channels containing isopropanol guests and running along the b-axis.
How are isopropanol guests incorporated into the hydrogen-bond network of the carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?

The carnosine linker twists to orient its amide and amine groups toward isopropanol. The guest forms O–H···O and N–H···O host–guest hydrogen bonds of 2.74 and 2.96 Å, respectively; a host–host N–H···O bond of 2.89 Å and carnosine–Zn(II) coordination provide additional stabilization.
How does the arrangement of isopropanol guests affect their contribution to the piezoelectric response of the carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The two isopropanol molecules in each channel have juxtaposed orientations, so their molecular dipoles may cancel instead of contributing to the piezoelectric response.
What Zn(II) coordination environment and framework connectivity occur in the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?

Deprotonated carboxylate and imidazole groups of carnosine coordinate tetrahedral Zn(II) centers. Each Zn(II) center is coordinated by a carboxylate group, an amino-terminal group, and two imidazole nitrogen atoms. Each carnosine linker connects four Zn cations, two of which are bridged by a deprotonated imidazole group, producing a permanent microporous scaffold.
What structural feature gives the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF conformational flexibility?
Flexible alkyl segments in the β-alanine–histidine peptide linker permit a wide range of conformations through low-energy torsional rearrangements.
What crystal morphology is observed for the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF, and what interaction is associated with its anisotropic growth?
It forms triangular-prism crystals. Suppression of anisotropic growth of the (020) surface along [001] is attributed to a shell of hydrogen-bonded ethanol molecules around the carnosine linker.
What Young’s modulus does DFT predict for the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
DFT predicts a Young’s modulus of 27 GPa.
What d16 piezoelectric strain coefficient does DFT predict for the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The predicted d16 coefficient is 5.5 pC/N.
How does the arrangement of ethanol guests affect their contribution to the piezoelectric response of the carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The two ethanol molecules in each channel have juxtaposed orientations, so their molecular dipoles may cancel instead of contributing to the piezoelectric response.
What role does ethanol play in assembling the ethanol-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF beyond serving as the reaction medium?
Ethanol acts as a structure-directing guest, embedding in the framework through guest–host interactions and affecting its morphology and atomistic packing.
What crystal morphology is adopted by the acetone-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
It forms rectangular-prism crystals.
What d16 piezoelectric strain coefficient does DFT predict for the acetone-solvated carnosine–zinc peptide MOF?
The predicted d16 coefficient is 11.2 pC/N.

What crystal system, space group, and layer stacking sequence characterize the crystals of the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand?

Its crystals are orthorhombic with space group Cmcm. Its layers adopt slipped AA stacking: neighboring layers are shifted along the b axis by about 2 Å, causing overlap of the aromatic cores while preventing direct stacking of the copper nodes.
What is the local coordination geometry of the copper nodes in the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand?

The copper nodes have a distorted pseudo-octahedral coordination environment. Four equatorial oxygen atoms form CuO4 linkages with Cu-O distances of about 1.9-2.0 Å, and two longer axial Cu-O contacts to oxygen atoms from adjacent layers have distances of about 3.2 Å.

What measured electrical conductivity and optical band gap classify the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand as a semiconductor?

Room-temperature four-probe conductivity measurements give about 0.10 S cm^-1, and solid-state UV-visible-near IR spectroscopy gives an indirect optical band gap of about 0.50 eV; the material is classified as a p-type semiconductor.

What charge carrier mobility is determined for the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand by terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, and what limits this value in the studied sample?
The terahertz time-domain spectroscopy-derived mobility is about 10.0 cm2 V^-1 s^-1 under ambient 300 K conditions. In the studied powder sample, grain-boundary scattering is the main limitation.

What does density-functional theory indicate about the preferred direction of charge transport in the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand, and what mechanism do temperature-dependent terahertz time-domain spectroscopy measurements indicate for the powder sample?

Density-functional theory indicates that charge transport is predominantly out-of-plane in the layer-stacked framework. Temperature-dependent terahertz time-domain spectroscopy of the powder sample indicates a thermally activated hopping-type charge transport mechanism.

What magnetic behavior is observed for the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand, and what does it indicate about interactions between its metal nodes?

It is paramagnetic. Magnetic-susceptibility measurements show a linear reciprocal susceptibility-versus-temperature behavior consistent with Curie-Weiss law, indicating antiferromagnetic interactions between neighboring copper nodes.

What textural properties does nitrogen adsorption-desorption measurement reveal for the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand?
Measured at 77 K, nitrogen adsorption shows that the material is nanoporous, with a Brunauer-Emmett-Teller surface area of 741 m^2 g^-1 and an estimated average pore size of about 1.23 nm.

What is the thermal stability of the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand, and what hydrate composition is suggested by thermogravimetric analysis?

It is thermally stable up to about 300 °C in an argon atmosphere. Thermogravimetric analysis shows a weight loss of about 7% at 100-150 °C, corresponding to three tightly bound water molecules per structural unit.

What oxidation state of copper and ligand redox form are indicated by spectroscopic analysis in the Cu2(OHPTP) two-dimensional conjugated metal-organic framework made from an octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene ligand?
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates predominantly Cu(II), and the octahydroxyphenanthrotriphenylene-derived linker is present in a semiquinone form.
What formula, formula weight, and elemental analysis percentages were obtained for crystalline [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n?

The crystallographically characterized material has formula C26H20N10NiSe2 and formula weight 689.13. Elemental analysis found C 45.30%, H 2.89%, N 20.35%, Ni 8.54%, and Se 22.91%; calculated values were C 45.32%, H 2.90%, N 20.33%, Ni 8.52%, and Se 22.92%.

What are the room-temperature crystal system, space group, unit-cell dimensions, and selected refinement parameters for the nickel(II) coordination polymer [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n?

It is triclinic, space group P -1, with a = 10.0171(3) Å, b = 12.3467(4) Å, c = 12.3812(4) Å, α = 96.085(2)°, β = 110.877(2)°, γ = 93.102(2)°, and V = 1415.71(8) Å^3. The density is 1.617 g cm^-3, R1(I > 2σ(I)) is 0.0481, and the goodness of fit on F^2 is 1.031.

In the single-crystal structure of [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n, what donor atoms surround the Ni(II) center, and are the selenium atoms of the selenocyanato ligands coordinated?

The Ni(II) center is hexacoordinated in an elongated octahedral environment formed by six nitrogen atoms. Four equatorial nitrogen donors come from the 1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene ligands, and two axial nitrogen donors are supplied by selenocyanato ligands; the selenium ends of the selenocyanato ligands remain uncoordinated.

What visible color change occurs when the nickel(II) coordination polymer [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n is treated with Hg2+ in aqueous medium, and which tested ions fail to produce this change?

The green crystals change to a grey material upon treatment with aqueous Hg2+. Among Pb2+, As3+, Hg2+, Ag+, and Cd2+, only Hg2+ alters the color; Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Zn2+, Al3+, and Fe3+ do not change the green color, and their FT-IR spectra after treatment remain identical to the spectrum of the untreated coordination polymer, indicating no detectable interaction.
In [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n, why are the uncoordinated selenium ends of the selenocyanato ligands proposed to be responsible for selective Hg2+ binding?

The selenocyanato ligands coordinate through their nitrogen atoms, leaving their selenium ends uncoordinated. Because Hg2+ has a well-known affinity for soft centres, it forms bonding interactions with these selenium ends, giving the selective response.
What FT-IR band change is observed after the nickel(II) coordination polymer [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n interacts with Hg2+, and what interaction does it support?

The band associated with the selenocyanato moiety shifts from 2070 cm^-1 in the original coordination polymer to 2145 cm^-1 after interaction with Hg2+. This shift supports bonding between the selenium end of the selenocyanato ligand and Hg2+.
What Hg-to-Ni ratio is indicated by EDX for the grey material formed when the nickel(II) coordination polymer [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n is treated with aqueous Hg2+?
EDX analysis of the mercury-loaded grey material indicates a Hg-to-Ni ratio of 2:1.
For the grey material obtained by treating [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n with aqueous Hg2+, what do EDX elemental maps show?
The EDX elemental maps confirm the presence of Hg and show a homogeneous distribution of Ni, Se, and Hg throughout the mercury-loaded material.
What does PXRD indicate about the material obtained when [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n absorbs Hg2+?
PXRD patterns indicate that crystallinity persists in the mercury-loaded material and that the framework remains stable after Hg2+ absorption.
What fluorescence-based detection limit for Hg2+ is obtained from aqueous suspensions of [Ni(1,4-bis(3-pyridyl)-2,3-diaza-1,3-butadiene)2(NCSe)2]n?
A detection limit of 1.68 × 10^-6 M was determined from fluorescence quenching titration of an aqueous suspension of the coordination polymer with Hg2+.
What single-crystal structural information defines the lithium-loaded state Li@Eu-C2O4?

Li@Eu-C2O4 crystallizes in the orthorhombic Cmmm space group. The asymmetric unit contains one crystallographically independent Eu3+ ion, two Li+ ions, half an oxalate C2O4^2- ion, one carbonate CO3^2- ion, and one mu2-O atom.
What are the two Li+ coordination sites in the single-crystal structure of Li@Eu-C2O4?

Li@Eu-C2O4 has two Li+ chelating sites. At the first site, a Li+ ion is coordinated by two opposing mu2-O atoms, with a Li-O distance of 2.01(9) Å and an O-Li-O angle of 180(1)°. At the second site, a Li+ ion is coordinated by oxalate and carbonate oxygen atoms, with Li-O distances of 1.97(17) Å and 1.98(2) Å and an O-Li-O angle of 101(1)°.
Why are the Li+-chelating sites in Li@Eu-C2O4 expected to favor Li+ over Na+?

The two Li+ chelating sites in Li@Eu-C2O4 have DFT-derived energy differences between Li+ and Na+ of 34.18 kJ mol^-1 for the first site and 56.86 kJ mol^-1 for the second site. The short Li-O distances, 1.97-2.02 Å, and the rigidity of the framework help fix these distances, producing a size-sieving effect that makes the sites suitable for Li+ rather than Na+.
What XPS evidence in Li@Eu-C2O4 supports Li+ uptake and Li-O coordination?
Li@Eu-C2O4 shows a Li 1s peak. In its high-resolution O 1s spectrum, an O-Li component is observed together with O-Eu and O-C components, indicating that oxygen atoms participate in Li+ coordination.
What framework architecture does the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water form?
It forms a three-dimensional catenated metal-organic framework composed of polycatenated two-dimensional layers with hxl topology.

For single-crystal X-ray data of the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water refined at 220 K, what solvent-region electron density was masked, and what guest content does it correspond to?
The masked solvent region corresponds to 1172 electrons per unit cell, consistent with 16 chloroform molecules and 16 water molecules per unit cell.

What average Fe-N bond lengths are measured for the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water at 220 K and 100 K, and what spin-state situation do these lengths indicate?
The average Fe-N bond lengths are 2.178(8) Å at 220 K and 2.081(11) Å at 100 K, indicating an incomplete spin transition.

At 220 K, what distances describe parallel pyridine-ring stacking and parallel naphthalene diimide center stacking in the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water?
The parallel pyridine rings have an interplanar distance of 3.397(10) Å and a center-to-center distance of 3.778(10) Å; the parallel naphthalene diimide centers are separated by 3.505(13) Å.

What two-dimensional-layer stacking pattern does the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water exhibit, and how many distinct naphthalene diimide-based bis-pyridyl ligand types are present in its asymmetric unit?
It exhibits an ABAB stacking pattern of the two-dimensional layers, and its asymmetric unit contains only one type of the N,N'-bis(4-pyridylmethyl)-1,4,5,8-naphthalene diimide ligand.
What magnetic spin-transition behavior does the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water exhibit?
It undergoes a gradual and incomplete thermal- and light-induced spin transition without hysteresis.
What dielectric behavior associated with spin-state switching does the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water show?
Its dielectric constant and dielectric loss vary with temperature, and the dielectric constant shows an abnormal increase synchronized with spin-state switching.

Under 355 nm excitation in temperature-dependent emission measurements, what spectral features and spin-state-related temperature behavior does the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water show?

It shows only a monomer naphthalene diimide emission peak around 460 nm and no observed excimer emission; the absence of excimer emission may be related to non-radiative transition pathways. Its monomer emission intensity varies with temperature and has an inflection at 220 K, indicating apparent coupling between luminescence and spin crossover.

What chloroform-related noncovalent interactions are present in the 100 K structure of the Au(I) cyanide-bridged Fe(II) catenated metal-organic framework solvated by chloroform and water, and how do they affect chloroform removal?

It contains hydrogen bonds between framework C-H groups and chloroform, and halogen bonds between chloroform Cl atoms and framework oxygen atoms; these interactions lead to removal of chloroform at an abnormally high temperature.

For the crystalline copper(II) coordination compound Cu-BDC-HMTA, where BDC denotes 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate and HMTA denotes hexamethylenetetramine, what is the composition of the asymmetric unit and the crystal space group?

The asymmetric unit contains two Cu(II) ions, one coordinated nitrate group, one fully deprotonated 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate ligand, one hexamethylenetetramine ligand, three water molecules (one coordinated and two free), and one coordinated hydroxyl group; the compound crystallizes in the monoclinic space group P21/n.
What pore window dimensions are present in the 2D layered framework of Cu-BDC-HMTA, where BDC denotes 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate and HMTA denotes hexamethylenetetramine?

What coordination geometries are present at the two independent Cu(II) centers in Cu-BDC-HMTA, where BDC denotes 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate and HMTA denotes hexamethylenetetramine?

One Cu(II) center adopts a five-connected distorted tetragonal-pyramidal geometry. The other Cu(II) center is six-coordinated with an octahedral geometry; its ligand donors are one nitrogen atom and five oxygen atoms, namely two oxygen atoms from two 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate ligands, two oxygen atoms from the same nitrate group, one oxygen atom from coordinated water, and the nitrogen atom from hexamethylenetetramine.
How are the Cu centers, 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate ligands, and hexamethylenetetramine ligands connected in the Cu-BDC-HMTA coordination compound, and what simplified supramolecular topology results?

The Cu centers, fully deprotonated 1,3-benzenedicarboxylate ligands, and hexamethylenetetramine ligands generate 1D chain and 2D bilayer structures; adjacent layers stack into a supramolecular architecture through hydrogen-bond interactions. Treating hexamethylenetetramine as linkers and the Cu centers as six-connected nodes, the structure simplifies to a pcu topology with point symbol {4^12.6^3}.
What coordination geometry surrounds Cu(II) in the as-synthesized hydrated copper MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

Each Cu(II) center is five-coordinate in a slightly distorted square-pyramidal geometry, with two carboxylate oxygen donors from 2,5-bis(prop-2-yn-1-yloxy)terephthalate, one coordinated water oxygen, and two nitrogen donors from 4,4′-bipyridine. The distortion parameter is τ = 0.05.
How do the organic linkers assemble the hydrated copper MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)] into an extended structure?

Monodentate carboxylate coordination from 2,5-bis(prop-2-yn-1-yloxy)terephthalate links the Cu centers into one-dimensional chains. Bridging 4,4′-bipyridine then connects these chains to form two-dimensional layers.
What stacking sequence and interlayer contacts characterize the two-dimensional layers in [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

The layers follow an ABCDABCD stacking sequence. Interlayer centroid-to-centroid distances of 4.06 and 6.22 Å occur between the terephthalate aromatic rings and 4,4′-bipyridine units. Possible alkyne–bipyridine π···π interactions and hydrogen bonding between an uncoordinated carboxylate oxygen and a methylene proton accompany this arrangement.
What happens when coordinated water is thermally removed from [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

Thermogravimetric analysis shows a 3.26% mass loss from 75 to 100 °C, assigned to removal of the coordinated water molecule. Decomposition begins above 212 °C. What infrared and isotope-exchange observations demonstrate that the coordinated water in [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)] is labile?

The coordinated-water band at approximately 3584 cm⁻¹ gradually weakens and disappears as the material is heated from 25 to 100 °C. After dehydrated crystals are soaked in D2O at room temperature for three days, a new coordinated-D2O stretching band appears near 2450 cm⁻¹.
Which UV–visible absorption features account for the blue color of [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?
The MOF has a ligand-centered n–π* absorption at 344 nm and a Cu-centered d–d absorption at 656 nm. Because the d–d band lies in the red region, the complementary observed color is blue.
What room-temperature photoluminescence is observed from [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)] under 330 nm excitation?
The material emits at approximately 390 nm under 330 nm excitation. The emission is assigned to an intraligand π–π* transition.
What magnetic behavior is shown by [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)] in variable-temperature susceptibility and magnetization measurements?

No magnetic ordering occurs down to 2 K. Curie–Weiss fits give θCW = −169(1) K in the high-temperature region and −2.61(1) K in the low-temperature region, indicating antiferromagnetic interactions. The room-temperature χMT value is 0.80 cm³ mol⁻¹, and the 2 K magnetization approaches 1 μB per formula unit above approximately 5.5 T.
What Cu(II) dimer arrangement and exchange parameter describe the nearest-neighbor magnetism of [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

The Cu(II) centers form magnetic dimers with a Cu···Cu separation of 5.3297(5) Å. Fitting the susceptibility with the Kahn-modified Bleaney–Bowers equation gives J = −32.68 meV, establishing antiferromagnetic nearest-neighbor coupling.
Under optimized ambient-pressure conditions, how does the copper MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)] catalyze cycloaddition of CO2 with epoxides?

After overnight preheating at 70 °C, 10 mg of the MOF was combined with 2 mmol of epoxide and 0.006 g of TBAB under 1 atm CO2 at room temperature for 18 h without solvent. What conditions and aldehyde-substituent trend characterize A3 coupling catalyzed by [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

The reaction uses 1 mmol each of an aromatic aldehyde, phenylacetylene, and 4-methylpiperidine with 10 mg of preheated MOF in 2 mL of dichloromethane at 40 °C under N2 for 7 h. What mechanism is proposed for propargylamine formation during A3 coupling catalyzed by [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N2)(H2O)]?

Phenylacetylene first forms a π-complex with a Cu center in the MOF. The aldehyde and secondary amine condense to form a Cu-bound iminium ion, which then couples with the activated phenylacetylene at the Cu center to produce the propargylamine.
What coordination environment surrounds Cu(II) in the anhydrous copper MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]?
Each Cu center is coordinated by two carboxylate oxygen donors and two nitrogen donors from 4,4′-azopyridine, producing a square-planar geometry. No water molecules are present in the structure.
How do the linkers assemble the anhydrous copper MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)] into an extended structure?

One type of one-dimensional chain is formed by Cu centers and 2,5-bis(prop-2-yn-1-yloxy)terephthalate, while another is formed by Cu centers and 4,4′-azopyridine. What N2-adsorption surface area does [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)] have at 77 K?
Its N2-adsorption surface area at 77 K is 2.57 m² g⁻¹.
Which UV–visible absorption bands are observed for [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]?
The material shows ligand-centered π–π* and n–π* absorption bands at 330 and 421 nm, respectively, together with a Cu-centered d–d transition near 664 nm.
How does [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)] perform in the solvent-free cycloaddition of CO2 with 2-methyl oxirane?

What catalytic result does [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)] give in A3 coupling of benzaldehyde, 4-methylpiperidine, and phenylacetylene?
Using 1 mmol of each reactant and 10 mg of the MOF in 2 mL of dichloromethane at 40 °C under N2 for 7 h gives 91% propargylamine yield, a TON of 684, and a TOF of 97.7 h⁻¹.
What Henry-reaction catalytic behavior does [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)] show under solvent-free conditions?

With 1 mmol of nitromethane, 3 mmol of aromatic aldehyde, and 15 mg of the MOF at 65 °C for 15 h, the framework catalyzes nitroaldol condensation through its Lewis-basic azo functionality. The highest yield is 93% with 4-nitrobenzaldehyde, and the catalyst remains active for four reuse cycles.
What magnetic interactions and exchange parameters characterize [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]?

The Cu(II) centers form isolated one-dimensional magnetic chains along the a-axis with a nearest-neighbor separation of 7.482(3) Å, and J′ = −0.28 meV indicates weak antiferromagnetic coupling.
What Cu(II) coordination and linker connectivity produce the three-dimensional framework of the monohydrated MOF [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O?

Each Cu(II) center is coordinated by three oxygen atoms and two nitrogen atoms in a distorted square-pyramidal geometry with τ = 0.33. What crystal system, space group, unit-cell parameters, and calculated density characterize [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O at 100 K?

The crystal is triclinic in space group P-1, with a = 9.7805(5) Å, b = 13.0164(7) Å, c = 13.0810(7) Å, α = 75.535(2)°, β = 79.241(2)°, γ = 79.306(2)°, and V = 1567.18(14) Å³. Its calculated density is 1.14 g cm⁻³.
What N2-adsorption surface area does [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O have at 77 K?
Its N2-adsorption surface area at 77 K is 7.6 m² g⁻¹.
How does the thermally activated form of [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O perform in the solvent-free cycloaddition of CO2 with 2-methyl oxirane?

Which framework functionality in [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O is proposed to provide Lewis-basic activity for the Henry reaction?
The free azo −N=N− group derived from the 4,4′-azopyridine linker provides Lewis-basic sites proposed to catalyze the base-catalyzed Henry reaction.
What magnetic behavior and Cu(II) dimer arrangement characterize [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O?

What room-temperature photoluminescence is observed from [Cu(C14H8O6)(C10H8N4)]·H2O under 330 nm excitation?

What crystallographic topology and cobalt coordination environment characterize the crystalline 2D cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework?

The framework crystallizes as a corrugated 2D layered structure in the triclinic P-1 space group with 3,6-connected kgd topology and interlayer slip-stacking. What thermal stability limit was obtained by thermogravimetric analysis for the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework?

What photocatalytic CO2-to-CO activity and selectivity are obtained for the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework under 10 W visible-light irradiation at 420 nm with Ru(Bpy)3Cl2 as photosensitizer and 1,3-dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1H-benzo[d]imidazole (BIH) as sacrificial electron donor?

Which in situ ATR FT-IR signatures are assigned to intermediates during visible-light CO2 reduction on the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework, and what role do cobalt clusters play?

The spectra show increasing *COOH intermediate peaks at 1513 and 1591 cm-1 and a *CO peak at 2065 cm-1 during visible-light CO2 reduction. Cobalt clusters mediate the formation of these species, facilitating electron-proton coupling.
What kinetic isotope effect was observed for photocatalytic CO2 reduction on the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework, and what rate-limiting step does it support?
A normal kinetic isotope effect greater than one was observed, supporting proton transfer in the formation of *COOH as the rate-limiting step.
What in situ XPS peak shifts occur for the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework after light irradiation, and what do they confirm?

After irradiation, the Co 2p1/2 and Co 2p3/2 peaks shift to lower binding energies by 0.25 and 0.12 eV, respectively, while the ligand N 1s and S 2p peaks shift to higher binding energies. These shifts confirm light-induced electron transfer from the organic ligand to the cobalt cluster.

What photocatalytic CO2-to-CO pathway is supported for the cobalt-coordinated phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate framework under visible-light irradiation with Ru(Bpy)3Cl2 as photosensitizer and 1,3-dimethyl-2-phenyl-2,3-dihydro-1H-benzo[d]imidazole (BIH) as sacrificial electron donor?

The pathway begins with electron donation from the phenothiazine-calix[3]arene carboxylate ligand to cobalt clusters, generating electron-dense cobalt sites. How is the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate synthesized, and what yield and crystal habit are obtained?

It is synthesized by heating the ligand, manganese(II) sulfate monohydrate, and water/methanol (1:1) in a sealed autoclave at 160 °C for 3 days, then cooling to 25 °C at 5 °C/h, affording colorless rod-like crystals in 30% yield based on manganese.

In the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate, what structural motifs are associated with proton-conduction sites and channels?

The framework is three-dimensional; three-fold bridging sulfate anions bridge manganese(II) centers and participate in hydrophilic channels, while uncoordinated carboxyl groups and water molecules are also associated with proton transport.

What is the best measured proton conductivity of the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate, and what structural and water-uptake features are associated with this value?

How does proton conductivity of the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate change with temperature at 98% RH and with relative humidity at 100 °C, and what low-temperature/low-humidity limitation is observed?

What are the activation energies for proton conduction in the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate at 68% and 98% RH, and what transport mechanisms do they suggest?

At 98% RH, the activation energy is 0.42 eV; this 0.4-0.5 eV range indicates a hybrid mechanism, combining Grotthuss transfer along hydrogen-bond networks built from entering water units and uncoordinated carboxyl oxygen atoms with vehicle migration of hydrated protons.
What thermal and water stabilities characterize the sulfate-bridged manganese(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate?

Thermogravimetric analysis in air shows that the framework remains stable up to 395 °C, with an observed solvent-molecule weight loss of 8.07% and a calculated value of 7.64%. For the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate, what are its framework dimensionality, space group, and unit-cell metrics?

In the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate, what structural features are associated with hydrogen-bonded proton-transport pathways?

For the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate under controlled humidity, what is its maximum proton conductivity, how does conductivity vary between 30 and 100 °C at 98% RH and between 68 and 98% RH at 100 °C, and what behavior is observed at 30 °C and 68% RH?

What are the apparent activation energies for proton conduction in the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate at 68% RH and 98% RH, and what proton transport mechanisms do these values support?

What solvent-accessible porosity and nitrogen adsorption metrics characterize the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate?

After one week of immersion in water, what changes are observed for the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate by powder X-ray diffraction and crystal morphology?
The powder X-ray diffraction peaks are virtually unchanged after one week of soaking in water, and the crystal morphology also changes little, indicating high water stability.

At 35 °C and P/P0 = 0.9, what water vapor adsorption capacity does the two-dimensional acetonitrile-solvated cobalt(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate exhibit?

For the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate, what crystallographic space group and unit-cell parameters does it have?

What total potential solvent-accessible volume does the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate have?

What feature of the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate provides free acidic protons in the lattice?
The terpyridine tricarboxylate ligand is only 67% deprotonated and coordinates metal cations, leaving free acidic protons from the partially protonated ligand within the lattice.

What infrared evidence indicates free carboxyl groups and water molecules in the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate?
The infrared spectrum shows bands associated with uncoordinated carboxyl groups near 1700 cm^-1, and a stretching vibration peak at 3403 cm^-1 is attributed to free water molecules.

What thermal stability limit and solvent weight loss are observed for the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate in air?
The framework remains stable up to 297 °C in air. Thermogravimetric analysis shows an observed solvent-molecule weight loss of 14.48%, compared with a calculated value of 12.63%.

Does the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate retain its structure after prolonged water exposure and after humidity-controlled electrochemical testing?

What Brunauer-Emmett-Teller surface area and mean adsorption aperture does the desolvated two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate show in nitrogen adsorption/desorption?

What activation energies are inferred for proton conduction in the two-dimensional water-containing nickel(II) framework derived from partially protonated 2-(6-phenyl-[2,3'-bipyridin]-4-yl)benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate at 68% and 98% RH, and what transport mechanisms do they indicate?

What crystal-integrity observations are made for the acetonitrile solvate of the one-dimensional copper(II) acetate porous coordination polymer that uses 3,6-di(pyridin-4-yl)-1,2,4,5-tetrazine as the organic linker, when it is prepared by solvent exchange with pure acetonitrile and then dried?

What linker orientation and guest-accessible volume characterize the acetonitrile solvate of the one-dimensional copper(II) acetate porous coordination polymer that uses 3,6-di(pyridin-4-yl)-1,2,4,5-tetrazine as the organic linker?

In the acetonitrile solvate, one of every three 3,6-di(pyridin-4-yl)-1,2,4,5-tetrazine linkers is tilted into the one-dimensional channels. The guest-accessible space is 181 Å^3, and the included acetonitrile guest volume is 46.4 Å^3.

What guest-linker interactions are present in the acetonitrile solvate of the one-dimensional copper(II) acetate porous coordination polymer that uses 3,6-di(pyridin-4-yl)-1,2,4,5-tetrazine as the organic linker, and what possible structural consequence do they have?

In the acetonitrile solvate, the acetonitrile guests form dimers through antiparallel dipole-dipole interactions and are linked through head-to-tail dipole-dipole interactions along the channel axis. What solid-state reflectance features are observed for the acetonitrile solvate of the one-dimensional copper(II) acetate porous coordination polymer that uses 3,6-di(pyridin-4-yl)-1,2,4,5-tetrazine as the organic linker, and what is proposed to give rise to its yellow colour?

The acetonitrile solvate shows two dominant reflectance peaks near 450 nm and 600 nm. The 450-nm peak is associated with Cu(II) centres in the framework, and the yellow colour is proposed to arise from coordination of the tetrazine-pyridine linker to the metal centres together with interlinker C-H...N interactions and host-guest interactions.
What is the topology and arrangement of the anionic oxalate-bridged layer and its templating cations in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

The anionic network, [Mn4Cl4Cr4(C2O4)12]n^8n-, is an irregular two-dimensional oxalate-bridged layer running parallel to (010), with a Shubnikov plane net fes topology designated (4·8²). The hydrogen-bonded dimethylethylammonium cations interleave between these anionic layers.
What space group and unit-cell parameters describe the single-crystal X-ray structure of the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer at 297(2) K?
It crystallizes in the polar monoclinic space group P21, with a = 13.8321(4) Å, b = 17.1042(4) Å, c = 20.4209(4) Å, alpha = 90°, beta = 91.874(2)°, gamma = 90°, V = 4828.7(2) Å^3, and Z = 2.
How are the chromium(III) centers coordinated and linked to manganese(II) ions in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

Each chromium(III) center is coordinated by six oxygen atoms from three bridging oxalate ligands in an approximately octahedral geometry. Each chromium(III) ion is linked to three manganese(II) ions, with two oxalate groups of the [Cr(C2O4)3] unit coordinated bidentately and one coordinated monodentately toward the manganese centers.
What ligands occupy the octahedral coordination sphere of Mn(II) in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

Manganese(II) is octahedrally coordinated by five oxalate oxygen atoms and one apical chloride: two oxygen atoms from one bis(bidentate) oxalate bridge, one oxygen atom from a monodentate-bidentate oxalate group, and two oxygen atoms from another bis(bidentate) oxalate bridge, together with the chloride. The shortest Mn-O distances correspond to monodentate coordination.
How do the dimethylethylammonium cations interact with the anionic Mn/Cr oxalate layer in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

The cations hydrogen-bond to oxygen atoms of the monodentate-bidentate oxalate groups and to chloride atoms coordinated to manganese(II). Four asymmetric dimethylethylammonium cations are linked by N-H···Cl interactions and the other four by two N-H···O_ox interactions.
What are the Cr-Mn distances through bis(bidentate) and bidentate-monodentate oxalate bridges in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

Through the bis(bidentate) oxalate ligand, chromium(III) and manganese(II) ions are separated by 5.4282(19)-5.5165(16) Å. Through the bidentate-monodentate oxalate bridge, the Cr-Mn distances are 5.2319(16)-5.3883(17) Å.
What is the interlayer distance in the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer, and how much water is taken up under humid conditions?

The interlayer distance is 8.55 Å, which is sufficient to accommodate several water molecules. After exposure to 80% relative humidity, thermogravimetric analysis shows a 4.16% weight loss below 130 °C, corresponding to five water molecules per formula unit in the interlayer space.
What are the observed air stability and solubility properties of crystals of the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?
The crystals are moderately air-stable and are very soluble in water but not soluble in common organic solvents.
What is the DC proton conductivity of the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer at 30 °C under dry nitrogen?
The impedance-derived DC conductivity is 7.75 × 10^-9 (Ω·cm)^-1 at 30 °C in dry nitrogen.

How does the proton conductivity of the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer vary with relative humidity, and what values are measured at 75%, 84%, and 90% relative humidity?

The conductivity increases by almost six orders of magnitude as relative humidity increases. At room temperature, the DC conductivity is 1.69 × 10^-7 (Ω·cm)^-1 at 75% relative humidity, 6.20 × 10^-4 (Ω·cm)^-1 at 84% relative humidity, and 1.60 × 10^-3 (Ω·cm)^-1 at 90% relative humidity; the 90% value corresponds to 22 °C.
What activation energy and proton-transport mechanism are indicated for the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer at 78% relative humidity?

The activation energy for proton conduction is 0.45 eV at 78% relative humidity. This value is slightly higher than typical for a dominant Grotthuss mechanism, so proton hopping is expected, with an additional contribution from direct diffusion of protons with water molecules in a vehicle mechanism.
What humidity-induced stability behavior is observed for the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer during conductivity measurements?

At 75% and 84% relative humidity, conductivity increases during the first 4 h and then remains relatively stable over 18 h. At 90% relative humidity, the material becomes deliquescent after 4 h. Powder X-ray diffraction after humidity exposure shows no structural changes.
What high-temperature Curie-Weiss parameters and magnetic interpretation are associated with the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

The Curie-Weiss fit of the high-temperature part of the inverse magnetic susceptibility gives C = (25.8 ± 0.2) emu K mol^-1 Oe^-1 and theta = (1 ± 1) K. The Curie constant is consistent with the paramagnetic state of manganese(II) and chromium(III) ions. The small Weiss parameter is not conclusive for weak magnetic interactions because of background-subtraction sensitivity and the limited high-temperature fitting range.

What magnetic phase transition is observed for the dimethylethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer, and how is its ground state related to the oxalate-bridged structure?

A magnetic phase transition occurs below 4.45 K, shown by splitting between zero-field-cooled and field-cooled magnetization curves. The ground state is described as ferromagnetic alternating Mn(II)/Cr(III) chains bridged by bis(bidentate) oxalate groups; these chains couple antiferromagnetically through bidentate-monodentate oxalate bridges to form antiferromagnetic planes, and weaker interlayer interactions produce long-range order. The high-field saturation magnetization is about 32 Bohr magnetons per formula unit. A weak ferromagnetic component from a canted antiferromagnetic sublattice is considered likely, because of anisotropic magnetic terms and locally non-centrosymmetric bridges.

For the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer, what is the topology of the oxalate-bridged anionic layer and how are the templating cations positioned relative to it?

The anionic network consists of irregular two-dimensional oxalate-bridged layers with a Shubnikov plane net fes topology designated (4·8²). Hydrogen-bonded diethylmethylammonium cations interleave the layers.
How are the chromium(III) centers coordinated and bridged in the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

Each chromium(III) center is coordinated by six oxygen atoms from three bridging oxalate ligands in an approximately octahedral geometry and is linked to three manganese(II) ions. Two oxalate groups are coordinated bidentately to manganese, and one oxalate group is coordinated monodentately.
What are the octahedral coordination environment and Mn-O/Mn-Cl distance features for manganese(II) in the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

Manganese(II) is octahedrally coordinated by oxalate oxygen atoms and an apical chloride. The Mn-O distances for a bis(bidentate) oxalate bridge are 2.203(7)-2.307(7) Å (average 2.248 Å), those for the monodentate oxalate oxygen of a monodentate-bidentate oxalate group are 2.164(7)-2.176(7) Å (average 2.167 Å), and the Mn-Cl distances are 2.416(3)-2.429(3) Å. The shortest Mn-O distance corresponds to monodentate coordination.
What are the interlayer spacing and adsorbed water content for the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer after humid exposure?

The heterometallic anionic layers are 8.67 Å apart, providing sufficient interlayer space for several water molecules. After exposure to 80% relative humidity, thermogravimetric analysis indicates a 3.00% weight loss below 130 °C, corresponding to four water molecules per formula unit in the interlayer space.
What low-humidity and high-humidity DC proton conductivities are observed for the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

In dry nitrogen (about 10% relative humidity) at 30 °C, the DC conductivity is 3.90 × 10^-7 (Ω·cm)^-1. At 22 °C and 94% relative humidity, it rises to 9.6 × 10^-4 (Ω·cm)^-1, an increase of almost four orders of magnitude with relative humidity.
What activation energy and proton-transport mechanism are inferred for the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

At 77% relative humidity, the activation energy for proton conduction is 0.51 eV. This value is slightly higher than typical for a dominant Grotthuss mechanism, so the conduction is interpreted as proton hopping with an additional contribution from water-mediated vehicle transport.
What magnetic transition and low-dimensional features are observed for the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer?

The magnetization versus temperature curve shows a magnetic phase transition at 4.45 K, marked by splitting between zero-field-cooled and field-cooled curves. A broad maximum slightly above this temperature is interpreted as a signature of low-dimensional magnetism, and the irreversibility below 4.45 K indicates long-range magnetically ordered behavior.
How is the magnetic ground state of the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer described?

The ground state is described as ferromagnetic spin chains of Mn(II) and Cr(III) ions bridged by bis(bidentate) oxalate groups that couple antiferromagnetically through monodentate-bidentate oxalate bridges, forming antiferromagnetic planes. Weaker interlayer interactions trigger long-range order below 4.45 K in a soft antiferromagnetic lattice. The high-field saturation magnetization of about 32 Bohr magnetons per formula unit supports ferromagnetic superexchange along the chains.

What Curie constant and Weiss temperature are obtained from high-temperature magnetic susceptibility for the diethylmethylammonium-containing oxalate-bridged [MnIICrIII] coordination polymer, and what caution applies to the Weiss value?

The Curie-Weiss fit of the high-temperature susceptibility gives C = (25.7 ± 0.2) emu K mol^-1 Oe^-1 and theta = (2.6 ± 0.8) K. The Curie constant is consistent with the paramagnetic state of Mn(II) and Cr(III). The small Weiss parameter and its large uncertainty, arising from fitting only the high-temperature region above 50 K, mean it cannot be used without doubt to infer negligible magnetic interactions.
What thermally accessible spin state does the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer exhibit, and what is the supported origin of that behavior?

It remains high spin down to 10 K; the small decrease of χMT below 20 K is attributed to zero-field splitting in Fe(II). The stable high-spin behavior is associated with strain produced by ligand dimerization, which acts on the Fe(II) chromophores and is transmitted through the crystal lattice.
How does high pressure modify the magnetic behavior of the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer?

Under high pressure, a thermally induced high-spin/low-spin crossover is restored. Increasing pressure first increases the low-spin fraction, but this increase practically stops above about 0.7 GPa, and the gradual spin crossover shifts to higher temperature. At 0.7-1.1 GPa, about 50% of the molecules remain low spin at lower temperatures, while a substantial low-spin fraction persists above 300 K; the residual high-spin fraction may arise from effective intrachain transmission of perturbations to neighboring spin-crossover centers, stabilizing high spin.

How can the low-spin state of the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer be generated at very low temperature, and how is the resulting hidden hysteresis characterized by subsequent heating and light irradiation?

At ambient pressure, the low-spin state is not generated by thermal cooling; it can be produced by irradiation with 808 nm light at 10 K, converting about half of the high-spin centers to low spin. On heating, a low-spin-to-high-spin transition occurs abruptly above about 40 K, with T1/2 = 47 K at 1 K min^-1, while cooling back to 10 K does not thermally induce high-spin-to-low-spin switching. What is the temperature dependence of the spin state in the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer, as measured by magnetic susceptibility?
It remains high spin over the investigated cooling range down to 10 K; a small reduction of χMT below 20 K is attributed to zero-field splitting in Fe(II).
What high-spin Fe-N distances and FeN6 octahedral shape distortion are present for the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer at 250 K?
The Fe-N distances are 2.187(1), 2.192(1), and 2.208(1) Å, with an average Fe-N distance of 2.196 Å. The shape-distortion parameter of the FeN6 octahedron is 0.065 at 250 K.
How many crystallographically independent Fe(II) centers are present in the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer?
There is one crystallographically independent Fe(II) center; the photoconverted structure does not crystallographically differentiate the Fe(II) centers.
What structural feature of the acetonitrile-solvated photoconverted Fe(II) coordination polymer is suggested to contribute to stabilization of its high-spin form besides ligand strain?

Intermolecular contacts involving coumarin fragments that are not part of the cyclobutane photocyclization remain in the polymer and facilitate transmission of perturbations to neighboring columns, suggesting crystal-lattice-based effects in addition to ligand strain can contribute to high-spin stabilization.
