S 2p peaks at 168.2 and 169.5 eV correspond to sulfate, while N 1s peaks at 398.8 and 400.7 eV are assigned to pyridine and pyrrole nitrogen, respectively.
What guest-solvent loss and thermal stability does as-synthesized Co4-Co-MOF show by thermogravimetric analysis?

Co4-Co-MOF loses approximately 20% of its mass before 130 °C, attributed to removal of N,N-dimethylformamide molecules trapped in the framework cavities. The framework remains intact up to about 400 °C, after which decomposition begins.
What density-functional-theory-derived oxygen evolution mechanisms and theoretical overpotentials were proposed for the Co4(SO4)4 cluster present in Co4-Co-MOF?

In the lower-overpotential pathway, a Co-O(sulfate) bond breaks and hydroxide binds to that Co site to form *OH(Co). A second *OH(Co) forms on another Co site, and successive dehydrogenation and coupling produce a Co-OO-Co intermediate before O2 desorption. Formation of the second *OH(Co) is the potential-limiting step, giving a calculated overpotential of 0.21 V. An alternative single-site pathway proceeds through high-energy *O(Co) and *OOH intermediates; *O(Co) formation is potential-limiting and gives an overpotential of 0.31 V.
What theoretical oxygen evolution reaction overpotential and potential-limiting step were calculated for the cobalt tetrakis(4-pyridyl)porphyrin sites in Co4-Co-MOF?
For the cobalt porphyrin sites, dehydrogenation of *OH to form *O(Co) is the potential-limiting step, with a calculated oxygen evolution reaction overpotential of 0.41 V.
How are the Co4(SO4)4 clusters connected in Co4-Cu-MOF, and what powder X-ray diffraction evidence supports the identity and phase purity of the bulk framework?

The clusters are linked by copper tetrakis(4-pyridyl)porphyrin units through bonds between cluster Co atoms and pyridyl N atoms. The measured powder X-ray diffraction pattern of bulk Co4-Cu-MOF matches the pattern calculated from its single-crystal structure, supporting the framework assignment and phase purity.
What coordination and sulfate-connectivity features define the Co4(SO4)4 cluster in Co4-Cu-MOF?

The cluster contains four chemically and symmetrically equivalent Co(II) ions. Each Co(II) ion is coordinated by four O atoms from three sulfate anions and two pyridyl N atoms, giving a six-coordinate octahedral environment. Each sulfate bridges three Co(II) ions in a μ3 mode, producing a distorted cube-like cluster.
What guest-solvent loss and thermal stability does as-synthesized Co4-Cu-MOF show by thermogravimetric analysis?

Co4-Cu-MOF loses approximately 20% of its mass before 130 °C, attributed to removal of N,N-dimethylformamide molecules trapped in the framework cavities. The framework remains intact up to about 400 °C, after which decomposition begins.
Why is the intermolecular copper-hydroxyl coupling pathway unlikely at the copper tetrakis(4-pyridyl)porphyrin linker sites in Co4-Cu-MOF during oxygen evolution?
The copper porphyrin units are spatially isolated in the framework, so two formal Cu(III)-OH species cannot readily approach one another for intermolecular coupling to form an O-O bond.
What density-functional-theory-predicted oxygen evolution mechanism and theoretical overpotentials were obtained for the Co4(SO4)4 cluster present in Co4-Cu-MOF?

The favored two-site pathway forms *OH(Co) intermediates on two Co sites, followed by dehydrogenation and coupling to produce a Co-OO-Co intermediate. Formation of the second *OH(Co) is potential-limiting and gives a calculated overpotential of 0.21 V. An alternative single-site pathway proceeds through a high-energy *O(Co) intermediate and has a calculated overpotential of 0.31 V.
In crystalline Co4-Zn-MOF, how are the Co4(SO4)4 clusters linked, and what coordination environment do the Co(II) ions have?

The clusters are linked by zinc tetrakis(4-pyridyl)porphyrin units through bonds between cluster Co atoms and pyridyl N atoms. Within each distorted cube-like cluster, the four Co(II) ions are chemically and symmetrically equivalent. Each Co(II) ion is coordinated by four sulfate O atoms and two pyridyl N atoms, giving a six-coordinate octahedral environment. Each cluster is connected to eight zinc porphyrin units.
What powder X-ray diffraction evidence supports the identity and phase purity of bulk Co4-Zn-MOF?
The measured powder X-ray diffraction pattern of bulk Co4-Zn-MOF matches the pattern calculated from its single-crystal structure, supporting the framework assignment and phase purity.
What does thermogravimetric analysis reveal about retained solvent and framework stability in as-synthesized Co4-Zn-MOF?

Co4-Zn-MOF loses approximately 20% of its mass before 130 °C, attributed to removal of N,N-dimethylformamide molecules trapped in the framework cavities. The framework remains intact up to about 400 °C, after which decomposition begins.

Under single-crystal X-ray diffraction at 100 K, what are the crystal system, space group, and unit-cell parameters of the [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O coordination polymer (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?

The material crystallizes in the triclinic system in space group P-1 with a = 7.0248(7) Å, b = 9.8275(12) Å, c = 11.2063(12) Å, α = 66.888(11)°, β = 73.749(9)°, γ = 84.612(9)°, cell volume = 683.01(14) Å³, and Z = 1.
What empirical formula and molecular weight correspond to the [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O coordination polymer (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?
Its empirical formula is C18H28Na2O23Zn2 and its molecular weight is 789.12.
What is the composition of the asymmetric unit in single-crystal [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?

It contains one Zn2+ ion, two halves of Na+ cations located at inversion centers, one benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linker, three coordinated water ligands, and two lattice water molecules, one of which has an occupation factor of 0.5.

What is the coordination number and bonding environment of the Zn2+ center in single-crystal [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate), and what Zn–O bond-distance range is observed?

The Zn2+ center is five-coordinate, bonded to one water molecule, two carboxylate oxygen atoms from two benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linkers, and two bridging water molecules; Zn–O distances are in the range 1.981(2)–2.196(2) Å.
What are the coordination numbers and Na–O bond-distance range for the sodium centers in single-crystal [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?
Both distinct Na+ centers are six-coordinate, bonded to oxygen atoms from water molecules and benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linkers, with Na–O distances in the range 2.335(2)–2.505(2) Å.
How does the benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linker coordinate to the metal centers and contribute to the structural dimensionality of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O?

All three carboxylate groups are deprotonated. The linker bridges Na+ and Zn2+ ions to form two-dimensional layers; one carboxylate group is uncoordinated and hydrogen bonds to coordinated water within each layer, while the other two are coordinated to metal centers. The layers are further connected by hydrogen bonding to build the crystal packing.
Which FT-IR bands in the fresh [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O coordination polymer (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) indicate carboxylate stretching modes and complete deprotonation of the linker?

Asymmetric carboxylate stretches appear at 1620 and 1544 cm^-1, and symmetric stretches appear at 1436 and 1364 cm^-1. The absence of bands in the 1680–1800 cm^-1 range indicates that the carboxylate groups of benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid are completely deprotonated.
What thermal events are observed in thermogravimetric analysis of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) from 25 to 800 °C under N2?

A first weight loss from 25 °C to about 162 °C is attributed to removal of water from the crystalline structure, calculated as 10%, and elimination of physically adsorbed solvent. Further decomposition occurs with heating, and the material loses 64.5% of its weight up to 800 °C.
What does agreement between simulated and experimental powder XRD patterns indicate for as-synthesized [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?
The similarity of the simulated and experimental powder XRD patterns indicates that the synthesized coordination polymer is pure.

When benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal (0.17 mmol) and malononitrile (0.33 mmol) are heated in ethanol (1 mL) with 2.5 mg of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) at 80 °C for 8 h, what conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal and selectivity toward benzylidene malononitrile are obtained?
The conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal is 100%, and the selectivity toward benzylidene malononitrile is 99%, as determined by GC analysis.

When benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal (0.17 mmol) and malononitrile (0.33 mmol) are heated in DMF (1 mL) with 2.5 mg of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) at 80 °C for 24 h, what conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal and selectivity toward benzylidene malononitrile are obtained?
The conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal is 98%, and the selectivity toward benzylidene malononitrile is 95%, as determined by GC analysis.

In a catalyst-removal experiment for the reaction of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal (0.17 mmol) and malononitrile (0.33 mmol) in DMF (1 mL) at 80 °C catalyzed by 2.5 mg of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate), the solid is removed after 4 h and the reaction is continued for 20 h. What conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal is obtained and what does it indicate?
The reaction gives 36% conversion of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal, indicating no significant catalyst leaching.

What evidence indicates that the structure of recovered [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) remains stable after use as a heterogeneous catalyst in the tandem deacetalization-Knoevenagel reaction?
The XRD pattern and FT-IR spectrum of the recovered material show that its structure remains unchanged after the reaction.

In NH3-TPD analysis of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) after degassing in N2 at 300 °C, NH3 adsorption, and heating to 400 °C, what acid-site desorption range and uptake are observed?
A desorption area from 84 to 345 °C is observed, associated with ammonia interaction with coordinatively unsaturated Zn2+ Lewis-acid sites; the uptake is 2290.8 μmol/g.

In CO2-TPD analysis of [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate) after degassing in N2 at 300 °C, CO2 adsorption, and heating to 400 °C, what basic-site desorption range and uptake are observed?

A small desorption area from 47 to 300 °C is observed, with an uptake of 48.9 μmol/g. This may reflect strong interactions of CO2 with basic sites, which would require higher temperatures for complete desorption; possible basic sites include oxygen atoms of polarized Na+-O2- bonds and free carboxylate groups of the benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linker.

What catalytic mechanism operates in the tandem deacetalization-Knoevenagel reaction of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal and malononitrile catalyzed by [NaZn(btc)(H2O)3]·1.5H2O (btc = benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate)?

Coordinatively unsaturated Zn2+ Lewis-acid sites promote deacetalization of benzaldehyde dimethyl acetal to benzaldehyde and activate the benzaldehyde carbonyl group. Malononitrile interacts with Lewis-basic sites, including oxygen atoms of polarized Na+-O2- bonds and an uncoordinated carboxylate group of the benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylate linker. The activated benzaldehyde and malononitrile then form benzylidene malononitrile.

In the crystal structure of the copper(II) metal-organic framework formed from 1-(3,5-dicarboxylatobenzyl)-4,4'-bipyridinium (Dcbb) and trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (Bpe) ligands, {[Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)]·Cl}, what are the crystal system and space group, and what species comprise the asymmetric unit?
It is triclinic and crystallizes in the centrosymmetric space group P-1. Its asymmetric unit contains one [Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)] unit and one chloride anion.

What donor atoms coordinate each Cu2+ center in the copper(II) metal-organic framework formed from 1-(3,5-dicarboxylatobenzyl)-4,4'-bipyridinium (Dcbb) and trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (Bpe) ligands, {[Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)]·Cl}, and what geometry results?

Each Cu2+ center is coordinated by two N atoms from a pair of Bpe ligands, two O atoms from bridging carboxylates, and one monodentate carboxylate O atom from a third Dcbb ligand, giving a trigonal-bipyramidal geometry.

In the copper(II) metal-organic framework formed from 1-(3,5-dicarboxylatobenzyl)-4,4'-bipyridinium (Dcbb) and trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (Bpe) ligands, {[Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)]·Cl}, how do carboxylate-bridged Cu dimers and Bpe ligands generate the 1D and 2D framework topology, and what adjacent-chain distance is reported?

A pair of μ-carboxylate bridges juxtaposes two Cu2+ centers into [Cu2(Dcbb)2] dimers, which extend into 1D chains along the a axis. Adjacent chains are about 11.1 Å apart, matching the length of a Bpe ligand (ca. 7.08 Å) plus two Cu-N contacts (ca. 2.0 Å each); the Cu-Bpe chains align along c and produce a 2D network in the ac plane.

Does the copper(II) metal-organic framework formed from 1-(3,5-dicarboxylatobenzyl)-4,4'-bipyridinium (Dcbb) and trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (Bpe) ligands, {[Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)]·Cl}, remain phase-pure after suspension in 20 mM Hepes buffer (pH 7.4) at room temperature for 12 h?

Yes. After sonication, 12 h standing, centrifugation, and vacuum drying, the PXRD pattern of the recollected framework agrees with the pattern simulated from its crystallographic data, indicating phase purity under these conditions.

What structural and electrostatic features are associated with the zwitterionic composition and cationic surface of the copper(II) metal-organic framework formed from 1-(3,5-dicarboxylatobenzyl)-4,4'-bipyridinium (Dcbb) and trans-1,2-bis(4-pyridyl)ethylene (Bpe) ligands, {[Cu(Dcbb)(Bpe)]·Cl}?

It is built from a zwitterionic Dcbb ligand containing aromatic rings and positively charged pyridinium centers, linked through Cu2+ nodes into a two-dimensional sheet with high surface exposure; its electrostatic surface is largely positive.

What crystal system, space group, and unit-cell parameters describe the crystal structure of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n at 170 K, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene?
The material is monoclinic in space group P-2yn, with a = 9.6904(5) Å, b = 17.7685(7) Å, c = 17.1919(9) Å, α = γ = 90°, β = 95.892(2)°, and V = 2944.5 Å³ at 170 K.

What is the local coordination environment of each cobalt(II) center in the crystal structure of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene?

Each cobalt(II) center is four-coordinate with a pyramidal {CoN₂O₂} environment, bonded to two oxygen atoms from deprotonated carboxylate groups of tib ligands and two nitrogen atoms from separate bimb ligands; bond angles about the cobalt center range from 96.18(11)° to 115.97(11)°.

What net topology is derived for the framework of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene?
The framework forms an uninodal net with point symbol (6⁵·8); its underlying net is described as a 4-connected sql topological type.

What happens to the structure of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, after immersion in water for 72 h?

After immersion in water for 72 h, the framework retains an integrated crystal form and its original structure, with no obvious changes in powder X-ray diffraction, indicating aqueous-phase stability.

What thermal decomposition steps are observed for the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, by thermogravimetric analysis under N2?

Thermogravimetric analysis under N2 shows two main losses: a 12.1% weight loss (calculated 10.7%) between 160 and 290°C due to loss of water molecules, followed by a large loss from 290 to 420°C probably caused by decomposition of the framework by loss of organic ligands; weight is then lost gradually up to 1000°C. The total mass loss is 82.3% (calculated 88.5%), corresponding to removal of organic species.

What optical absorption edge and band gap are measured for powder samples of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, by UV–vis diffuse reflectance?
Powder samples show a steep absorption edge at 360 nm in the UV region and a band gap of 3.96 eV.

In the UV-irradiation photocatalytic degradation tests of methylene blue (MB) and methyl violet (MV), what degradation percentages does the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n achieve after 120 min when 10 mg is dispersed in 50 mL of 6 mg L⁻¹ dye solution, after 24 h of dark adsorption, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene?
Under these conditions, the material degrades 92.1% of MB and 89.3% of MV after 120 min of UV irradiation.

Which active species is identified as dominant in the UV photocatalytic degradation of methylene blue (MB) and methyl violet (MV) by the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, from radical-trapping experiments?

Hydroxyl radicals (·OH) are the main active species. Adding isopropanol sharply reduces degradation for this material (MB to 66.7% and MV to 64.6% after 120 min), whereas EDTA-2Na has almost no effect.

At approximately what potential versus NHE does the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, catalyze water oxidation under weakly alkaline conditions, and what oxygen-evolution overpotential is observed at pH 8.06?
It catalyzes water oxidation around 1.2 V vs NHE, and at pH 8.06 the oxygen-evolution overpotential is 405 mV.

How does the onset potential for electrocatalytic water oxidation by the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, vary with pH, and what transfer process is indicated?
The onset potentials vary linearly with pH, with a slope of -44.6 mV pH⁻¹; this suggests a possible proton-coupled electron-transfer (PCET) process.

What dissolved O₂ concentration and current density are obtained for the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene, during controlled-potential electrolysis of water oxidation at 1.30 V and pH 8.06?

Over 2000 s at 1.30 V and pH 8.06, the material gives a dissolved O₂ concentration up to 390.7 μM and a current density of 2.93 mA cm⁻²; the current remained settled during the 2000 s, indicating stable catalysis over this period.

At an overpotential of 404.6 mV for electrocatalytic water oxidation, what is the calculated Faraday efficiency of the cobalt(II) coordination polymer {[Co(tib)2(bimb)2]·4H2O}_n, where tib = 3-((4-(1H-1,2,4-triazol-1-yl)benzyl)oxy)benzoic acid and bimb = 1,4-bis(imidazole-1-ylmethy) benzene?
The calculated Faraday efficiency is 66.69%.
What coordination topology and crystallographic space group characterize crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate with formula Ni3(BTC)2·12H2O, where BTC = 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate?

Crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate contains nickel ions in separate octahedral sites and forms zigzag chains built from two symmetry-nonequivalent tetra-aqua Ni(II) units and 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligands. It crystallizes in a monoclinic system with space group C2 (No. 5).

When crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate is placed in a TEM chamber and exposed to a 200 kV electron beam, what transformation occurs and what is the chemical nature of the nanoparticles produced?

The material first amorphizes rapidly while retaining the 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligand and coordination bonds. Continued electron-beam exposure breaks the coordination bonds and transforms it, within tens of seconds, into a nanomaterial composed of crystalline metallic Ni nanoparticles embedded in an organic matrix. Ni L3 and L2 electron-energy-loss edges at about 855 and 872 eV confirm the metallic Ni character, and chemical mapping shows nickel localized in the matrix while oxygen is distributed through the volume.
How do electron-beam current density and sample temperature affect Ni nanoparticle growth in the organic matrix formed from crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate under 200 kV HRTEM?

At 200 kV, Ni nanoparticles in the organic matrix reach an average diameter of 4.2 nm after 100 s at 65 pA cm^-2 and about 6.3 nm after 100 s at 120 pA cm^-2. At -110 °C and 50 pA cm^-2, growth starts after about 54 s and reaches about 3 nm after 70 s.
What HRTEM time-evolution features indicate where metallic Ni nanoparticles grow in the organic matrix formed from crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate?

The metallic Ni nanoparticles show essentially constant lattice parameters within measurement error, constant lattice orientation in space, and constant spatial position over time. These features indicate nucleation and growth at fixed positions inside the original framework rather than translational motion.

What do confocal Raman and photoluminescence measurements reveal about the 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligand and coordination bonds during amorphization and electron-beam modification of crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate?

The initial crystal shows Raman bands at 700–1800 cm^-1 from the organic part and lower-frequency bands at 200–250 cm^-1 attributed to coordination bonds and metal-cluster vibrations. After amorphization and electron-beam modification, Raman intensities decrease and the 200–250 cm^-1 coordination bands disappear, while photoluminescence red-shifts and develops a broad band near 500 nm. Carbon-related Raman modes at 1320 and 1570 cm^-1 appear only at a much higher electron dose, indicating that the examined electron-beam-modified material retains the intact 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligand while losing coordination-bond signatures.
How stable is the photoluminescence signal of electron-beam-modified nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate after four months under ambient conditions?

After four months at ambient conditions, the electron-beam-modified material shows a photoluminescence signal similar to the as-prepared material, with only a slightly disturbed shape that may be due to ongoing amorphization.
What metal-cluster topology feature of crystalline nickel 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate is proposed to favor metallic Ni nanoparticle formation during electron-beam modification?

In this framework the nickel-oxygen polyhedra are separate and do not share joint metal-oxygen-metal vertices. Electron-beam action is proposed to break Ni-ligand coordination bonds more readily than joint metal-oxygen-metal bonds in the metal cluster, leading to crystalline metallic Ni nanoparticles in the organic matrix.
What composition and framework structure characterize crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate with formula Co3(BTC)2·12H2O, where BTC = 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate?

The framework contains cobalt ions in separate octahedral sites and forms zigzag chains built from two symmetry-nonequivalent tetra-aqua Co(II) units linked by 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligands. It crystallizes in the monoclinic space group C2 (No. 5).
What immediate structural effect does placement in a TEM vacuum chamber have on crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate single crystals?

Upon placement in the TEM vacuum chamber, the single crystals amorphize almost immediately, while the 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligand and coordination bonds are retained, as indicated by Raman and photoluminescence spectroscopy.
What product forms when crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate is subjected to intensified 200 kV electron-beam exposure, and how is the cobalt phase identified?

Intensified 200 kV electron-beam exposure first amorphizes the crystal and then produces a nanomaterial containing crystalline metallic Co nanoparticles inside an organic matrix. Co L3 and L2 electron-energy-loss edges centered near 780 and 795 eV without oxygen signal identify the nanoparticles as metallic cobalt, while oxygen remains distributed through the matrix.

How quickly does electron-beam exposure at room temperature produce metallic Co nanoparticles in the organic matrix from crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate, and what average particle size is reached at 120 pA cm^-2?
At room temperature and 120 pA cm^-2, metallic Co nanoparticles grow on a timescale of about one minute, reaching an average diameter of approximately 4 nm after 68 s.
What HRTEM observations indicate that Co nanoparticles grow on fixed sites inside the organic matrix formed from crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate?

The growing metallic Co nanoparticles show essentially constant lattice parameters within measurement error, constant lattice orientation in space, and constant spatial position over time, indicating nucleation and growth at fixed positions inside the original framework.
What spectroscopic evidence indicates that electron-beam-modified crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate retains an intact organic ligand while losing coordination-bond signatures?

Photoluminescence spectra of the modified material show features associated with amorphization, including a red shift and a broad band near 500 nm attributed to loss of long-range crystal order. Together with Raman spectra indicating that coordination-bond vibrations disappear and with evidence for cobalt nanoparticle formation, these observations support retention of the 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate ligand while coordination bonds are lost.
What metal-cluster topology feature of crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate is proposed to favor metallic Co nanoparticle formation during electron-beam modification?

In this phase the cobalt-oxygen polyhedra are separate and do not share joint metal-oxygen-metal vertices. Electron-beam action is proposed to break cobalt-ligand coordination bonds more readily than joint metal-oxygen-metal bonds, leading to metallic Co nanoparticles inside the organic matrix.
Which crystal system and space group characterize the crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate phase assigned to CCDC 2167623?
It crystallizes in the orthorhombic system with space group P2_1 2_1 2_1 (No. 19).
What solid-to-solid transformation and product are observed when the crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate phase assigned to CCDC 2167623 is exposed to a 200 kV electron beam?

Electron-beam exposure transforms this phase into an organic matrix containing crystalline cobalt oxide nanoparticles. The solid-to-solid transformation associated with oxide-nanoparticle formation proceeds on a timescale of approximately 30 min.

What nanoparticles form when the crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate phase assigned to CCDC 2167623 is modified by a 200 kV electron beam, and what metal-cluster structural feature is associated with their oxide chemistry?

The modification produces cobalt oxide nanoparticles inside an organic matrix. EELS detects both cobalt L-edges and oxygen K-edges, confirming an oxide state; the exact cobalt oxidation or oxide-phase assignment is not fully resolved. The oxide product is associated with a framework in which metal-oxygen polyhedra share at least one oxygen vertex. Electron-beam treatment is proposed to break metal-ligand bonds while retaining joint metal-oxygen-metal bonds, and DFT calculations estimate specific-position Co-O bonds in this phase to be about 40% stronger than other Co-O bonds in the same phase.
What HRTEM time-resolved characteristics describe cobalt oxide nanoparticle growth in the organic matrix formed from the crystalline cobalt 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate phase assigned to CCDC 2167623?

Within the first few minutes, the growing oxide nanoparticles appear in an unstable mode: their size, shape, and position change chaotically; interlayer distances evolve during growth; and transient mechanical rotations of the nanoparticles are observed.
Under what solvothermal conditions is the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework obtained, and what crystal appearance and yield result?

The framework is obtained by combining 6-quinolinecarboxylic acid and copper nitrate trihydrate in N,N-dimethylformamide and acetonitrile, sonicating the mixture in a sealed 10 mL glass vial, heating at 100 °C for 72 h, and cooling naturally, which gives dark green rhombic block crystals in 65% yield based on 6-quinolinecarboxylic acid.
What crystal system, space group, and unit-cell parameters are obtained for single crystals of the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework at 293 K?
It crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group P21/c, with a = 9.9241(10) Å, b = 16.5632(13) Å, c = 13.3988(9) Å, β = 96.690(8)°, and cell volume 2187.4(3) Å³ at 293 K.
What local coordination geometry and Cu–O and Cu–N distances are found for copper ions in the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?

Each copper ion has approximately square-pyramidal coordination, bound to four carboxylate oxygen atoms and one quinoline nitrogen atom, with Cu–O distances of 1.950–1.977 Å and a Cu–N distance of 2.190 Å.
What secondary-building units and framework dimensionality characterize the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?
The framework is constructed from paddle-wheel dinuclear copper clusters, [Cu2(COO)4], linked by carboxylate-containing ligands to form a two-dimensional framework.
How does coordination of the 6-quinolinecarboxylate ligands generate Lewis basic sites in the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?

The two crystallographically distinct ligands have different coordination modes: one uses both the carboxylate group and the quinoline nitrogen for copper coordination, whereas the other coordinates only through its carboxylate group, leaving the quinoline nitrogen uncoordinated; these uncoordinated nitrogen atoms provide Lewis basic sites.
What interlayer interaction is present in the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework, and what distance characterizes it?
π–π interactions occur between benzene rings of adjacent two-dimensional layers at approximately 3.77 Å, helping link the layered structure into a three-dimensional arrangement.
What pore or channel features are observed in the crystal structure of the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?
Along the a-axis, the structure has rectangular channels about 4 Å × 8 Å, and the calculated solvent-accessible volume is 29.6%.
What does powder X-ray diffraction indicate about the crystallinity and phase purity of the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?
The diffraction pattern of finely ground synthesized material matches the simulated pattern well, indicating high crystallinity and high phase purity.
What infrared spectral change supports coordination of the 6-quinolinecarboxylate carboxylate group to copper in the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework?
The C=O stretching vibration of the carboxyl group shifts from 1700 cm⁻¹ in free 6-quinolinecarboxylic acid to 1680 cm⁻¹ in the framework, supporting carboxylate coordination to copper.
What X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy Cu 2p features are observed for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework, and what copper oxidation state do they support?
Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 peaks appear at 932.6 eV and 952.3 eV, respectively, consistent with Cu(II).
What thermal behavior is observed for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework by thermogravimetric analysis under nitrogen?

An initial 11.3% weight loss between 30 and 165 °C is attributed to gradual removal of guest solvent molecules, followed by a sharp decrease starting at 245 °C indicating framework collapse, consistent with good thermal stability.
How does the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework respond to immersion in different solvents, as judged by powder X-ray diffraction?

After immersion for up to 24 h, the material retains its structural integrity in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) used for synthesis. In dimethylacetamide, dichloromethane, acetonitrile, dimethyl sulfoxide, methanol, and ethanol, powder X-ray diffraction peaks shift noticeably, but re-immersion in DMF restores the original pattern; the reversible changes are suggested to arise from solvent effects on weak interlayer interactions such as π–π contacts or hydrogen bonding.
What textural properties are obtained for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework from nitrogen adsorption-desorption at 77 K?
It exhibits a Type I nitrogen adsorption isotherm characteristic of microporosity, with a calculated Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface area of 317.6 m²/g and a pore volume of 0.1731 cm³/g.
What atmospheric-pressure CO2 uptake is observed for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework at 298 K?
It adsorbs 28.7 cm³/g of CO2 at atmospheric pressure and 298 K.
What optimized conditions and model-reaction yield are used for copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework-catalyzed oxazolidinone formation from CO2 and N-benzylprop-2-yn-1-amine?

Using 0.5 mmol N-benzylprop-2-yn-1-amine, the framework at 4.7 mol% based on copper, 0.1 mmol tetrabutylammonium iodide, 0.5 mL N,N-dimethylformamide, atmospheric CO2, and 30 °C for 10 h gives 99% oxazolidinone yield.

What representative substrate scope and oxazolidinone yields are obtained for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework catalyzing CO2 with propargylic amines under 0.5 mmol substrate, 4.7 mol% framework based on copper, 0.1 mmol tetrabutylammonium iodide, 0.5 mL N,N-dimethylformamide, atmospheric CO2, and 30 °C for 10 h?

Methyl- and methoxy-substituted propargylic amines give 91% and 99%, respectively; a tert-butyl-substituted substrate gives 82%; thiophene- and pyridine-containing substrates give 98% and 57%, respectively; and N-propyl and N-butyl terminal propargylamines give 61%.
In a gram-scale reaction of N-benzylprop-2-yn-1-amine with CO2 catalyzed by the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework, what yield and product mass are obtained?
Starting from 1.02 g (7 mmol) of N-benzylprop-2-yn-1-amine, the reaction gives 1.31 g of 3-benzyl-5-methyleneoxazolidin-2-one in 99% yield.
How does the catalytic activity and crystallinity of the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework change over five consecutive oxazolidinone-formation cycles?

The framework maintains high activity over five cycles, with yields of 99%, 94%, 92%, 91%, and 90%; powder X-ray diffraction patterns after recycling remain consistent with the original material, indicating that the framework is maintained.
What mechanism is proposed for the copper(II) 6-quinolinecarboxylate framework-catalyzed carboxylative cyclization of CO2 with propargylic amines?

The proposed mechanism begins with CO2 adsorption and enrichment in the porous framework. Uncoordinated quinoline nitrogen atoms may act as Lewis-base sites that assist deprotonation of the propargylic amine N–H group, while Cu(II) activates the alkyne through a copper–π interaction. CO2 insertion into the activated nitrogen forms a carbamate; nucleophilic attack of an oxygen on the alkyne carbon gives cyclization; and proton-assisted demetallation releases the oxazolidinone product while regenerating the catalyst.
What crystallographic parameters describe the single-crystal structure of the La-MOF built from nitrilotrisbenzoate and 1,4-bis(1-imidazole)benzene ligands?

At 267 K, the La-MOF crystallizes in the monoclinic system with space group P2₁/c; the unit cell is a = 14.540(8) Å, b = 23.286(11) Å, c = 24.683(10) Å, α = γ = 90°, β = 100.212(17)°, and V = 8225(7) Å³, with Mo Kα radiation at λ = 0.71073 Å.

What are the coordination geometries of the two distinct La sites in the La-MOF, one coordinated by ten oxygen atoms from six nitrilotrisbenzoate (NTB3-) ligands and the other coordinated by eight oxygen atoms from five NTB3- ligands and one nitrogen atom from a 1,4-bis(1-imidazole)benzene (bib) ligand?

The ten-oxygen, six-ligand environment is a ten-coordinated {LaO10} hexadecahedron with a twisted four-hat triangular-prism configuration. The eight-oxygen, one-nitrogen environment is a nine-coordinated {LaO8N} tetrakaidecahedron with a twisted three-hat triangular-prism configuration.
What are the La-O and La-N bond distances in the La-MOF constructed from nitrilotrisbenzoate and 1,4-bis(1-imidazole)benzene ligands?
The La-O distances range from 2.461(9) to 2.984(9) Å, and the La-N distance is 2.663(12) Å.
How do the nitrilotrisbenzoate (NTB3-) and 1,4-bis(1-imidazole)benzene (bib) ligands contribute to the extended framework of the La-MOF?
The La-MOF forms a two-dimensional network viewed along the b-axis, and interaction between the NTB3- and bib ligands constructs a three-dimensional channel structure along the c-axis.
How is the phase purity of the as-synthesized La-MOF assessed?
The powder X-ray diffraction pattern of the as-synthesized La-MOF matches the simulated pattern derived from the single-crystal data, indicating good phase purity.
What aqueous pH stability does the La-MOF exhibit?
The La-MOF maintains luminescence stability in aqueous solution over the pH 2–12 range.
What solid-state fluorescence emission does the La-MOF display, and how is it assigned?

Upon excitation at 395 nm, the La-MOF shows a broad emission peak at 475 nm, appearing as blue luminescence assigned to π→π* or n→π* electron transitions of the nitrilotrisbenzoic acid (H3NTB) ligand.
What fluorescence decay components characterize the La-MOF, and what do they indicate?
The decay curve fits a double-exponential function with components at 1.55 μs and 10.34 μs, indicating ligand-based luminescence in the framework.
What Stern–Volmer quenching constant and detection limit apply to Fe3+ sensing by the La-MOF?
For Fe3+ sensing, the Stern–Volmer quenching constant is 8.6 x 10^4 M^-1, and the detection limit calculated by the 3σ/Ksv method is 1.29 x 10^-6 M.
What evidence and mechanism are proposed for Fe3+-induced fluorescence quenching of the La-MOF?

The La-MOF remains structurally intact after Fe3+ recognition, indicating that fluorescence quenching is not caused by framework collapse. Its excitation peak overlaps the Fe3+ absorption band at 250–400 nm, so Fe3+ can absorb part of the excitation light and inhibit energy transfer from the ligand to the metal center. After Fe3+ exposure and elution, elemental mapping still shows Fe in the framework, supporting Fe3+ binding.
What Stern–Volmer quenching constant and detection limit apply to PO43- sensing by the La-MOF?
For PO43- sensing, the Stern–Volmer quenching constant is 5.42 x 10^3 M^-1, and the detection limit is 1.59 x 10^-6 M.
What mechanism is proposed for PO43--induced fluorescence quenching of the La-MOF?

Powder X-ray diffraction shows that the La-MOF structure remains intact after PO43- addition, so quenching is not caused by framework collapse. The UV–visible absorption of PO43- in the 300–400 nm region overlaps the excitation band of the La-MOF, suggesting competitive energy absorption may cause the fluorescence quenching.
What fluorescence response and Stern–Volmer parameters apply to p-Nitroaniline sensing by the La-MOF in ethanol solution?

In ethanol solution, p-Nitroaniline significantly reduces the fluorescence intensity of the La-MOF to 2.24 x 10^4 a.u., corresponding to 82.51% quenching efficiency. The Stern–Volmer quenching constant is 1.22 x 10^4 M^-1, and the detection limit is 1.32 x 10^-6 M.
What mechanisms are proposed for p-Nitroaniline-induced fluorescence quenching of the La-MOF?

p-Nitroaniline absorbs part of the excitation light used for the La-MOF because its UV–visible absorption overlaps the La-MOF excitation near 390 nm; this restricts ligand-to-metal energy transfer and gives competitive energy absorption. Density-functional calculations indicate that the lowest π* orbital of p-Nitroaniline is closest to and lower than the corresponding orbital of the nitrilotrisbenzoate (NTB3-) antenna ligand, allowing photoexcited electrons to transfer to the p-Nitroaniline LUMO and preventing their return to the valence band, which supports fluorescence quenching by photoinduced electron transfer.
What weight-loss steps occur in thermogravimetric analysis of the La-MOF?

The La-MOF shows two apparent weight-loss steps: a first loss of 3.11% (calculated 3.18%) before 201°C, followed by a second loss from 205 to 545°C attributed to decomposition of the framework; the framework quickly disintegrates after this second step.
What components are present in the asymmetric unit of the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units in its as-crystallized state?

The asymmetric unit contains one tetrathiafulvalene-derived carboxylate ligand, one Cd2+ ion, one 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene molecule, one coordinated acetic acid molecule, and one water molecule.
What framework dimensionality and anthracene-ligand orientation characterize the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units?

The 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene ligand lies nearly vertically relative to the tetrathiafulvalene-containing two-dimensional layer, and the complete framework forms a 3-fold interpenetrated three-dimensional structure.
What near-infrared absorption is exhibited by the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units?
It shows wide and strong absorption around 900 nm and broad near-infrared absorption from about 800 to 1200 nm, associated with charge-transfer interactions in its donor-metal-acceptor framework.

In the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) analysis of the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units, with a lanl2dz basis set applied to the cadmium center, where are the HOMO and LUMO located?
The HOMO is located in the central core of the tetrathiafulvalene unit, while the LUMO is distributed on the 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene ligand.

What temperature rise and photothermal conversion efficiency does the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units achieve under 808 nm irradiation at 0.7 W cm-2?

Under 808 nm irradiation at 0.7 W cm-2, the temperature reaches 196 °C in 5 s and a maximum of 201 °C, with a photothermal conversion efficiency of 35.7%; the rise from 25 °C to 201 °C occurs within 7 s.
What thermal stability does the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units show by thermogravimetric analysis?

It shows high thermal stability: the main framework changes occur at approximately 270 °C, possibly because of partial framework collapse caused by hydrogen-bond breakage, and rapid weight loss occurs only by about 350 °C.
What redox peaks are observed for the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units by cyclic voltammetry?
It exhibits two pairs of reversible redox peaks corresponding to the tetrathiafulvalene (TTF)/TTF+ and TTF/TTF2+ couples.
How stable is the cadmium-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units under repeated 808 nm laser on/off cycling and after three weeks?

Under repeated 808 nm laser on/off cycles at 0.4 W cm-2, it heats rapidly from 25 °C to 127 °C, remains undecomposed after five cycles, and after three weeks shows almost no change in photothermal performance; powder X-ray diffraction after the measurements indicates retained crystallinity.

In the as-crystallized cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units, what coordination environment and ligand connectivity produce its two-dimensional framework?

The Co2+ center is six-coordinate; the asymmetric unit contains one-half of a tetrathiafulvalene-derived carboxylate ligand, one Co2+ ion, one-half of a 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene molecule, and one coordinated water molecule. Each tetrathiafulvalene-derived carboxylate ligand bridges two Co2+ ions, with Co-O distances of 2.0733(5)-2.1319(5) Å and a Co-N distance of 2.1674(6) Å. The tetrathiafulvalene-derived carboxylate and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene ligands extend along the ab plane to form a two-dimensional layer with regular cavities.

What noncovalent contacts are present in the two-dimensional stacking of the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units, and what effect do they have?

Its two-dimensional stacking includes a short C-H...pi contact of 2.6786(70) Å and hydrogen-bond contacts, including O...H-O at 2.2991(38) Å and S...H-C at 2.9687(19) Å; these contacts promote interlayer interaction forces and energy transfer between the layers.

What thermal events and framework-collapse temperatures are shown for the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units by thermogravimetric analysis?

It loses about 20% of its mass around 230 °C, then loses mass rapidly around 270 °C, which is attributed to collapse of the framework; rapid weight decrease occurs by about 350 °C, and the material shows high thermal stability.
What reversible redox features are observed for the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units in cyclic voltammetry?
It exhibits two pairs of reversible redox peaks corresponding to the tetrathiafulvalene (TTF)/TTF+ and TTF/TTF2+ couples.
What near-infrared absorption is exhibited by the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units, and what interaction does it indicate?

It shows wide and strong absorption around 900 nm, including a relatively large near-infrared peak, which indicates significant charge transfer within its donor-metal-acceptor framework and supports its use in near-infrared photothermal conversion.

In the B3LYP/6-31G(d,p) analysis of the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units, with a lanl2dz basis set applied to the cobalt center, where are the HOMO and LUMO located?
The HOMO is mainly located in the central core of the tetrathiafulvalene moiety, while the LUMO is distributed on the carboxylbenzene portion around another tetrathiafulvalene unit.

Under 808 nm laser irradiation at 0.7 W cm-2, what photothermal temperature increase is obtained for the cobalt-based metal-organic framework containing tetrathiafulvalene and 9,10-di(pyridin-4-yl)anthracene units?
Its temperature increases from 22 °C to 99 °C in 5 s, reaching a maximum temperature of 105 °C.
What space group and Zr6-cluster connectivity characterize BUT-30?
BUT-30 crystallizes in cubic Fm-3m and contains 12-connected Zr6 clusters.
What nitrogen adsorption behavior and values characterize BUT-30 at 77 K?
At 77 K, BUT-30 shows a type I nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherm and is microporous, with total N2 uptake of 745 cm3 g-1, a BET surface area of 2653 m2 g-1, and pore sizes of 1.5 nm.
What Zr6-cluster topology forms when the room-temperature Cu-Zr bimetallic MOF crystallizes from Zr4+, isonicotinic acid, and Cu+ in DMF?
The product forms an 8-connected reo framework. Reversible Cu-pyridyl bond formation and dissociation support crystallization at room temperature under kinetic control.
What space group and linker connectivity characterize the room-temperature Cu-Zr bimetallic MOF formed from Zr4+, isonicotinic acid, and Cu+ in DMF?
The MOF crystallizes in primitive cubic Pm-3m, with each Zr6 cluster connected to eight Cu-pyridyl linkers derived from isonicotinic acid.

What copper oxidation states and counterion identity are established for the room-temperature Cu-Zr bimetallic MOF formed from Zr4+, isonicotinic acid, and Cu+ in DMF, and what limitation remains for the equatorial Cu sites?

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy shows a mixture of Cu(I) and Cu(II), with a Cu(I)/Cu(II) ratio of 4.7. Cl− counterions are assigned using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and elemental analysis. Equatorial counterions and solvent molecules on the Cu-pyridyl units could not be refined because of disorder.
What low-angle PXRD reflection is observed for the room-temperature Cu-Zr bimetallic MOF crystallized from Zr4+, isonicotinic acid, and Cu+ in DMF, and what does it indicate?
A low-angle reflection near 4.1 degrees assigned to the (110) diffraction is observed; its appearance indicates the reo framework.
How does the as-synthesized room-temperature Cu-Zr bimetallic MOF formed from Zr4+, isonicotinic acid, and Cu+ in DMF respond to water and solvent-removal activation?
It decomposes readily in water, shown by disappearance of its PXRD peaks. Activation was unsuccessful even using supercritical CO2, which is attributed to weak Cu-pyridyl coordination bonds.

In the as-synthesized DMF-solvated cobalt(II)-organic framework containing anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylate as the dicarboxylate co-ligand, what are the Co(II) coordination geometries and the channel architecture of the framework?

The framework has two crystallographically independent Co(II) centers, each four-coordinate with distorted tetrahedral geometry. The 1,3,5-tris(4-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)phenyl)benzene ligands and sulfate anions form a three-dimensional network; two-fold interpenetration of these networks along the c direction creates rhombic channels. The anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylate co-ligands occupy these rhombic channels and link the interpenetrating nets, producing a self-penetrating framework.

When the as-synthesized DMF-solvated cobalt(II)-organic framework containing anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylate as the dicarboxylate co-ligand is immersed in water, what response is observed, and what framework feature inhibits dissociation of the dicarboxylate co-ligand in the presence of water?

The sample showed no visible change and no detected change in the Co(II) coordination environment after one week in water. The bulky anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylate backbone further confines the rhombic channels, creating a relatively stable interaction between the co-ligand and the framework that inhibits co-ligand dissociation in the presence of water.
For the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn, what composition and monoclinic crystallographic parameters define its crystalline state?

It has formula C16H15N3O8SZn and formula weight 474.74, crystallizes in the monoclinic system in space group P2_1/n, and has a = 12.9657(5) Å, b = 8.0690(3) Å, c = 18.3612(8) Å, α = γ = 90°, β = 109.516(5)°, V = 1810.60(14) Å^3, Z = 4, and density 1.742 g cm-3.

What components form the asymmetric unit of the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn, and how do the N-(3-carboxypyridin-2-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand and sulfate connect the Zn centers to give its layered framework?

The asymmetric unit contains one Zn(II) ion, one sulfate anion, one N-(3-carboxypyridin-2-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand, and two lattice water molecules. Adjacent Zn(II) ions are alternately bridged by pyridyl N atoms and carboxylate O atoms of this ligand to form a 1D chain, and μ2-sulfate anions connect adjacent chains into a 2D layer with a 6^5.8 topology.
How stable is the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn when soaked in common solvents for 24 h, as assessed by PXRD?

After 24 h immersion in DMF, ethanol, acetone, dichloromethane, water/DMF (1:1), water/acetone (1:1), and water/ethanol (1:1), it retains good chemical stability: PXRD diffraction peaks and crystallinity do not change, although peak intensities vary.
What thermal weight-loss behavior is observed for the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn during TGA under air at 10 °C min-1?
The TGA curve shows two regions of weight loss: an initial loss of about 7.70% between 65 and 135 °C, and continuous weight loss beginning above 320 °C.
What color change and response time are observed for solid C16H15N3O8SZn under xenon-lamp irradiation?

The material shows a rapid, naked-eye-detectable photochromic change from light yellow to green upon xenon-lamp irradiation, with the color becoming saturated within 60 s; it also exhibits reversible photochromism.
What irradiation-induced UV-vis bands appear for the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn, and what mechanism do the spectroscopic results suggest for its photochromism?

After irradiation, new visible absorption bands around 427, 599, and 714 nm emerge and their intensities increase with irradiation time. Together with EPR evidence, these bands suggest that photochromism arises from photoinduced radical generation.
What dihedral angles are observed between the pyridinium ring and adjacent pyridyl rings in the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn?
The dihedral angles are 8.362° and 11.277°.
What is the proposed origin of the ammonia vapochromic behavior of the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H15N3O8SZn, and why is it not attributed to a structural or radical process?

The behavior is proposed to arise from synergistic host–guest interactions with ammonia. It is not attributed to a structural phase change because powder XRD patterns of the original and ammonia-exposed material remain essentially unchanged, and it is not attributed to radical formation because the ammonia-exposed material is EPR silent.
For the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn, what crystal system, space group, and structural dimensionality does it adopt?
It crystallizes in the monoclinic system, space group Cc, and forms a chain structure.
What components make up the asymmetric unit of the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn?
The asymmetric unit contains one Zn(II) ion, one sulfate anion, one N-(4-carboxypyridin-3-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand, two coordinated water molecules, and three lattice water molecules.

What Zn(II) coordination geometry is adopted in the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn, and how does the N-(4-carboxypyridin-3-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand connect the metal centers?

The Zn(II) ion adopts a distorted octahedral geometry. It is chelated and bridged by pyridyl N atoms and carboxylate O atoms of the N-(4-carboxypyridin-3-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand, producing a 1D chain.
Are the 1D chains in the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn further extended by sulfate anions?
No; the chain skeletons are not further extended by terminal sulfate anions.

How do water molecules, sulfate oxygen atoms, and the carboxylate oxygen of the N-(4-carboxypyridin-3-yl)-4,4'-bipyridinium ligand assemble the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn into a three-dimensional supramolecular network?

Water molecules form a linear water dimer and a water trimer. The sulfate oxygen atoms and the carbonyl oxygen atom of the ligand act as hydrogen-bond acceptors for these water clusters, generating a dense hydrogen-bonded 3D supramolecular architecture.
How stable is the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn after soaking in common solvents for 24 h, as assessed by PXRD?

It is stable in DMF, ethanol, acetone, dichloromethane, water/DMF (1:1), water/acetone (1:1), and water/ethanol (1:1) after 24 h; PXRD shows unchanged crystallinity, with only variations in peak intensities.
At what temperature does the residual framework of the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn begin to decompose under air thermogravimetric analysis?
The residual framework begins to decompose above 333°C.
What naked-eye photochromic color change does the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn undergo under xenon-light irradiation, and how quickly does the coloration saturate?
It changes from light yellow to green, and the coloration saturates after irradiation within 60 s.
Which new visible-region absorption bands emerge for the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn after xenon irradiation, and how do their intensities evolve with irradiation time?
Bands around 412, 429, and 728 nm emerge, and their intensity progressively increases as the irradiation time increases.

What evidence supports the interpretation that the photochromic color change of the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn is associated with photoinduced radical formation rather than an irradiation-induced structural change?

After irradiation, new visible bands appear and EPR signals consistent with photoinduced radicals are obtained, while the original and irradiated materials have essentially unchanged PXRD patterns; this supports a radical color change rather than an irradiation-induced structural change.
What are the dihedral angles between the pyridinium ring and adjacent pyridyl rings in the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn?
The dihedral angles are 36.029° and 36.651°.
Why does the Zn(II) coordination polymer with formula C16H21N3O11SZn not exhibit ammonia vapochromism under ammonia vapor exposure?
Ammonia molecules have difficulty interacting with the Lewis acidic pyridinium nitrogen and the coordinatively saturated Zn(II) centers, so the material does not show a chromic response.
What host–guest structural feature is observed in the SF6-loaded single-crystal structure of Ni(ina)2?
SF6 molecules pack within one-dimensional channels of Ni(ina)2, and the pore environment is well matched to SF6 so that SF6 forms strong, multipoint van der Waals contacts with the framework.
What powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) feature appears when Ni(ina)2 adsorbs SF6, and what cause is assigned to that feature?
A [020] diffraction peak appears in the PXRD pattern of SF6-loaded Ni(ina)2; this change is attributed to SF6 adsorption altering the internal and external linings of the pores.
What thermal-release behavior is observed for a saturated SF6-loaded Ni(ina)2 sample, and what does it indicate?

After SF6 saturation and two days at room temperature, SF6-loaded Ni(ina)2 loses about 30% of its mass when heated to 400°C, whereas desolvated Ni(ina)2 shows no weight loss below 400°C; in situ TG-FTIR-MS detects SF6 release, with the SF6 signal first increasing and then decreasing as release completes, indicating strong host–guest interactions between SF6 and the Ni(ina)2 framework.
What SF6 and N2 host–guest distances are predicted by grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) and density-functional theory (DFT) calculations for Ni(ina)2?

The fluorine atoms of SF6 are predicted to be 2.74–3.18 Å from hydrogen atoms on the pyridyl rings, whereas the nitrogen atoms of N2 are predicted to be 3.09–4.51 Å from framework hydrogen atoms; the shorter SF6 contacts indicate stronger SF6–framework interactions.
What molecular-simulation binding energies are predicted for SF6 and N2 in Ni(ina)2, and how do they compare with the measured low-coverage isosteric heats of adsorption?

The predicted binding energies are 59.08 kJ mol-1 for SF6 and 18.82 kJ mol-1 for N2. The measured zero-coverage isosteric heats of adsorption are 33.4 kJ mol-1 for SF6 and 16.1 kJ mol-1 for N2, and the simulated and experimental ordering are consistent.
What crystal system and space group characterize Ce-FDM-50, and what powder X-ray diffraction evidence supports its phase purity?

Ce-FDM-50 crystallizes in the orthorhombic space group Cmca. Its experimental powder X-ray diffraction pattern agrees with the pattern simulated from its single-crystal structure, supporting phase purity.
What is the coordination environment of cerium in Ce-FDM-50, and what is the reported Ce–O bond-length range?

Each Ce(III) center is eight-coordinate, bound to two carboxylate oxygen atoms, two meta-phenolic oxygen atoms, and two para-phenolic oxygen atoms from gallic-acid linkers, plus two oxygen atoms from coordinated DMF molecules. The Ce–O bond lengths range from 2.42 to 2.61 Å.
What mixed carboxylate–pyrogallate paddle-wheel secondary building unit forms in Ce-FDM-50, and what structural parameters characterize it?

Two Ce(III) ions separated by 3.92 Å are bridged by two carboxylates along two diagonal directions and two pyrogallates along the other two directions. The resulting paddle-wheel unit has a slightly distorted square-planar geometry, an 82.3° dihedral angle between the paddles, and functions as a 4-connected node.
How are the paddle-wheel secondary building units connected in Ce-FDM-50, and what role do the coordinated DMF molecules play?

The paddle-wheel units are connected through the phenyl rings of the gallic-acid linkers to form a two-dimensional framework with sql topology. The coordinated DMF molecules are terminal ligands occupying remaining Ce(III) coordination sites and do not connect the secondary building units.
What layer packing and interlayer distance characterize Ce-FDM-50, and how does chloride contribute to charge compensation?

The two-dimensional layers stack in an ABA sequence along the [010] direction and have an interlayer distance of 5.59 Å. A chloride counterion compensates framework charge and forms an O–H···Cl hydrogen bond with a meta-phenolic hydroxyl group at a distance of 2.95 Å.
What does Ce 3d X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicate about the cerium oxidation state in Ce-FDM-50?
Ce 3d X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy indicates that cerium is present only as Ce(III); the characteristic Ce(IV) feature near 914.0 eV is absent.
What FT-IR evidence supports deprotonation of the para-phenolic hydroxyl group of the gallic-acid linker in Ce-FDM-50?

The 3494 cm⁻¹ band assigned to the intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded pyrogallol O–H stretch is absent from Ce-FDM-50, supporting deprotonation of the para-phenolic hydroxyl group upon framework formation.
What happens when Ce-FDM-50 is activated to remove coordinated DMF, and how do the treatments affect its crystallinity and porosity?

After dichloromethane exchange and evacuation at room temperature or 150 °C, digestion ¹H NMR gives a DMF:gallic-acid-linker ratio of 1.94:1, close to the theoretical 2:1, while powder X-ray diffraction shows that the framework remains intact. At 200 °C, the ratio falls to 1.36:1, but 68% of the DMF remains and the framework undergoes complete phase transformation. Thermogravimetric analysis shows no coordinated-DMF loss below 190 °C and gradual weight loss above 190 °C, consistent with structural collapse. Coordinated DMF therefore cannot be removed without destroying the framework, and no meaningful nitrogen uptake is observed at 77 K.
What structural motif, topology, and layer packing characterize Eu-FDM-50?

Carboxylate and pyrogallate groups from gallic-acid linkers coordinate pairs of Eu(III) ions into paddle-wheel secondary building units. The units are joined through phenyl rings into two-dimensional square layers with sql topology and ABA packing.
How was the phase purity of Eu-FDM-50 established?

The structure of single-crystalline Eu-FDM-50 was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, and its experimental powder X-ray diffraction pattern matched the pattern simulated from that structure, confirming phase purity.
What framework topology and layer packing characterize Nd-FDM-50?

Nd-FDM-50 forms two-dimensional square layers with sql topology, in which paddle-wheel secondary building units act as nodes and the phenyl rings of gallic-acid linkers act as edges. The layers adopt ABA packing.
Which groups of the gallic-acid linker form the paddle-wheel secondary building unit in Nd-FDM-50?
The carboxylate and pyrogallate groups of gallic acid co-coordinate pairs of Nd(III) ions to form the paddle-wheel secondary building units.
What crystallographic evidence supports the phase purity of Nd-FDM-50?
The experimental powder X-ray diffraction pattern of Nd-FDM-50 matches the pattern simulated from its single-crystal structure, indicating a phase-pure crystalline product.
